title: The Ugly Duckling
description: A despised grey duckling endures winter and becomes a beautiful swan.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

The stork was walking about on his long red legs, chattering in Egyptian, for that is the language he had learned from his mother. All around the fields and meadows were great woods, and in the midst of the woods deep lakes. Yes, it was indeed glorious out in the country. In the midst of the sunshine there lay an old manor house, with deep canals round it, and from the wall down to the water there were great burdocks, so high that little children could stand upright under the loftiest of them. It was just as wild there as in the deepest wood, and here sat a Duck upon her nest. She had to hatch her ducklings; but she was almost tired out before the little ones came; and she sat so long on them, that they at last hatched. One after another, the little ducks came creeping out. 'Quack! quack!' said they, and they all came out as fast as they could, looking all around them under the green leaves; and the mother let them look as much as they liked, for green is good for the eyes. 'How large the world is!' said the young ones, for they certainly had much more room now than when they were in the eggs. 'Do you think this is all the world?' said the mother. 'Oh, it extends far beyond the other side of the garden, quite into the parson's field; but I have never been there. Are you all here?' and she stood up. 'No, not all; the largest egg is still there. How long will this last? I am quite tired of it.' And she sat down again. 'Well, how are you getting on?' asked an old Duck, who had come to pay her a visit. 'There's one egg that takes a long time,' said the Duck who sat there; 'it will not break. But now let us look at the others. They are the prettiest little ducks I ever saw. They are all like their father; the rogue, he never comes to see me.' 'Let me see the egg that will not break,' said the old Duck. 'You may be sure that it is a turkey's egg. I was once cheated in the same way, and I had great anxiety and trouble with the young ones, for they are afraid of the water. I could not get them to venture in. I quacked and clucked, but it was no use. Let me see the egg. Yes, that is a turkey's egg. Leave it alone, and teach the other children to swim.' 'I think I will sit on it a little longer,' said the Duck. 'I have sat so long already that I may as well sit a few days more.' 'Just as you please,' said the old Duck; and she went away. At last the great egg broke. 'Pip! pip!' said the young one, and crept out. It was very large and ugly. The Duck looked at it. 'That is a very great, ugly duckling,' said she; 'it does not look at all like the others: can it really be a turkey chick? Well, we shall soon find out. It must go into the water, even if I have to push it in.' The next day the weather was splendid, and the sun shone brightly on the green burdocks. The mother Duck with all her family went down to the canal. Splash! she jumped into the water. 'Quack! quack!' she said, and one duckling after another plunged in. The water closed over their heads, but they came up again in an instant, and swam beautifully; their legs went of themselves, and they were all in the water, even the ugly grey one. 'No, it is not a turkey,' said the old Duck; 'see how nicely it uses its legs, and how upright it holds itself. It is my own child! On the whole it is quite pretty, when you look at it properly. Quack! quack! now come with me, and I will take you into the world, and introduce you in the duck-yard; but keep close to me, so that no one may tread on you, and take care of the cats.' So they came to the duck-yard. There was a terrible noise there, for two families were quarreling about an eel's head, and in the end it was carried off by the cat. 'See, that is the way of the world,' said the mother Duck, and she whetted her beak, for she too wanted the eel's head. 'Only use your legs,' she said. 'See that you can bustle about, and bow your heads before the old Duck yonder. She is the most distinguished of all here; she is of Spanish blood, and that is why she is so fat; and do you see, she has a red rag round her leg; that is considered extremely fine, and is the greatest distinction a duck can have. Don't turn in your toes; a well-bred duckling spreads his feet wide apart, just like father and mother, so. Now bend your necks, and say 'quack.'' And they did so; but the other ducks round about looked at them, and said quite loud: 'Look there! now we are to have another brood, as if there were not enough of us already; and — fie! — how ugly that one is! We will not endure that!' And immediately one of the ducks flew at him, and bit him in the neck. 'Let him alone,' said the mother; 'he is not doing any one any harm.' 'Yes, but he is so large and so strange,' said the duck who had bitten him; 'and therefore he must be turned out.' 'Those are pretty children that the old one has,' said the old Duck with the rag round her leg. 'They are all pretty except one, and that has not turned out well. I wish she could hatch it over again.' 'That cannot be done, my lady,' said the mother Duck. 'It is true that he is not handsome, but he is a very good child, and swims as well as the others, indeed a little better. I think he will grow handsome, and become smaller in time. He stayed too long in the egg, and therefore is not properly formed.' And then she scratched his neck and smoothed his feathers. 'Moreover, he is a drake,' she said, 'and therefore it does not matter so much. I think he will be very strong: he is getting on already.' 'The other ducklings are graceful enough,' said the old Duck. 'Make yourself at home, and if you find an eel's head, be so kind as to bring it to me.' So they made themselves at home. But the poor duckling, who had come last out of the egg, and who was so ugly, was bitten and pushed and made fun of, as much by the ducks as by the chickens. 'He is too big!' they all said. And the turkey-cock, who had been born with spurs, and therefore thought himself an emperor, puffed himself up like a ship with sails, and walked up to him, and gobbled, and grew quite red in the face. The poor duckling did not know where he dared to stand or walk; he was quite miserable because he was so ugly, and was the jest of the whole duck-yard. So it went on the first day, and afterwards it became worse and worse. The poor duckling was chased and buffeted about by all; even his brothers and sisters behaved unkindly to him, and were always saying: 'May the cat take you, you ugly creature!' And the mother said: 'I wish you were far away!' And the ducks bit him, and the chickens pecked him, and the girl who fed the poultry kicked him with her foot. Then he ran and flew over the fence, and the little birds in the bushes flew up in alarm. 'That is because I am so ugly,' thought the duckling, and shut his eyes, but ran on still. At last he came to a great moor, where the wild ducks lived. There he lay the whole night, and he was very tired and sorrowful. In the morning the wild ducks came up, and looked at their new comrade. 'What sort of a duck are you?' they asked, and the duckling turned himself in all directions, and bowed to them in the best way he could. 'You are terribly ugly,' said the wild ducks, 'but that does not matter to us, if you do not marry into our family.' Poor thing! he had never thought of marrying; he only wanted leave to lie among the reeds and drink some of the water. He lay there two whole days; then came two wild geese, or rather two wild ganders. They had not been long out of the shell, and were very saucy. 'Hark ye, comrade,' said they; 'you are so ugly that we like you very well. Will you go with us, and become a bird of passage? Not far from here, in another moor, there are some pretty wild geese, all unmarried, and all able to say 'Honk!' You are ugly enough to make your fortune among them.' 'Bang!' went a gun all at once, and both the wild ganders fell dead among the reeds, and the water became red with blood. 'Bang!' went a gun again, and whole flocks of wild geese flew up from the reeds. And then another bang went off. A great hunt was going on. The hunters lay in ambush all round the moor, and some were even sitting in the trees, and looking over the reeds. The blue smoke rose up like clouds among the dark trees, and was wafted far away over the water; and the hunting dogs came splash, splash, into the moor, and the reeds and the rushes bent down on every side. How frightened the poor little duckling was! He turned his head, and wanted to hide it under his wing, but at that moment a great terrible dog stood close by the duckling. His tongue was hanging out of his mouth, and his eyes gleamed horribly. He thrust his nose close to the duckling, showed his sharp teeth, and then, splash, splash! he went on, without seizing him. 'Oh, Heaven be thanked!' sighed the duckling. 'I am so ugly that even the dog will not bite me!' And so he lay quite still, while the shot rattled through the reeds, and gun after gun went off. It was late in the day before it became quiet; but the poor little thing did not dare to get up. He waited several hours more before he looked round him, and then hastened away from the moor as fast as he could. He ran over fields and meadows, and there was such a wind that he had hard work to make his way. Towards evening he reached a poor little hut. It was so dilapidated that it did not know on which side to fall, and that is why it remained standing. The wind whistled round the duckling in such a way that he had to sit down to hold himself, and it became worse and worse. Then he noticed that the door had lost one of its hinges, and hung so crookedly that he could creep through the crack into the room. An old woman lived there with her cat and her hen. The cat, which she called her little son, could arch his back, and purr, and give out sparks when he was stroked the wrong way. The hen had quite short legs, and was therefore called 'Chickie-short-legs'; she laid good eggs, and the old woman loved her as her own child. In the morning the strange duckling was at once noticed, and the cat began to purr, and the hen to cluck. 'What is that?' said the old woman, and looked round; but her eyes were not good, and she thought the duckling was a fat duck that had strayed. 'That is a capital capture!' said she. 'I hope it is not a drake. We must see.' So the duckling was taken on trial for three weeks, but no eggs came. And the cat was master of the house, and the hen was mistress, and they always said: 'We and the world!' for they thought they were half the world, and by far the better half. The duckling thought one might have a different opinion, but the hen would not allow it. 'Can you lay eggs?' she asked. 'No.' 'Then you will please hold your tongue.' And the cat said: 'Can you arch your back and purr and give out sparks?' 'No.' 'Then you had better not have an opinion when sensible people are speaking.' And the duckling sat in a corner and was in low spirits; then he began to think of the fresh air and the sunshine, and was seized with a strange longing to swim on the water, so that he could not help telling the hen about it. 'What is the matter with you?' she asked. 'You have nothing to do, and that is why you get these fancies. Either lay eggs or purr, and you will get over them.' 'But it is so delightful to swim on the water,' said the duckling, 'and so refreshing to feel it close over your head when you dive to the bottom.' 'That would be a great pleasure indeed!' said the hen. 'I think you have gone mad. Ask the cat about it — he is the wisest animal I know — ask him if he likes to swim on the water or to dive under it. I say nothing about myself. Ask our mistress, the old woman; no one in the world is wiser than she. Do you think she would like to swim and let the water close over her head?' 'You do not understand me,' said the duckling. 'We do not understand you! Then who is to understand you? Do you want to be wiser than the cat and the old woman? I will not say anything of myself. Don't be so conceited, child, and thank your Maker for all the kindness you have received. Are you not in a warm room, and have you not society around you from which you can learn something? But you are a chatterer, and it is not pleasant to have to do with you. You may believe me, I speak for your good. I tell you disagreeable things, and by them you may know your friends. Only take care that you learn to lay eggs, or to purr and give out sparks.' 'I think I will go out into the wide world again,' said the duckling. 'Yes, do go,' said the hen. So the duckling went away. He swam on the water, and dived under it, but he was slighted by every creature because he was so ugly. Now came the autumn; the leaves in the forest turned yellow and brown; the wind caught them so that they danced about, and the air was very cold. The clouds hung low, heavy with hail and snow, and the raven stood on the fence and croaked. The poor duckling was certainly not in good spirits from the cold. One evening, just as the sun was setting with unusual brilliancy, a flock of beautiful large birds came out of the bushes. The duckling had never seen anything so beautiful. They were dazzlingly white, with long, graceful necks. They were swans. They uttered a singular cry, spread out their magnificent broad wings, and flew away from the cold regions to warmer lands, to open lakes. They mounted so high, so high! And the ugly little duckling felt quite strangely as he watched them. He turned round and round in the water like a wheel, stretched out his neck towards them, and uttered such a loud and strange cry that he frightened himself. Oh! he could not forget them, those beautiful, happy birds; and when he was out of sight of them, he dived to the very bottom, and when he came up again he was quite beside himself. He did not know what the birds were, nor whither they flew; but he loved them as he had never loved anything before. He did not envy them at all; how could he think of wishing to be so beautiful? He would have been glad if the ducks had only endured him among them, the poor, ugly creature! And the winter was so cold, so cold! The duckling had to swim about in the water to keep it from freezing; but every night the hole in which he swam became smaller and smaller. Then it froze so hard that the ice cracked; and the duckling had to use his legs to keep the hole open. At last he became exhausted, and lay quite still, and thus froze fast in the ice. Early in the morning a peasant came by, and when he saw what had happened, he broke the ice in pieces with his wooden shoe, and carried the duckling home to his wife. There it revived. The children wanted to play with it, but the duckling thought they wanted to hurt him, and in his fright jumped up into the milk-pan, so that the milk spurted out into the room. The woman clapped her hands, and he flew into the butter-tub, and then into the meal-barrel and out again. What a sight it was! The woman screamed, and struck at him with the fire-tongs; the children ran races to catch him, and laughed and shouted. Fortunately the door stood open, and the duckling flew out among the bushes and snow, and lay there in the snow, quite exhausted. But it would be too sad to tell all the misery and privation which the poor little duckling had to endure in the hard winter. He was lying on the moor among the reeds, when the sun began to shine warm again; the larks sang, and beautiful spring had come. Then all at once the duckling could flap his wings. They beat the air more strongly than before, and bore him away quickly, and before he well knew it, he was in a large garden, where the apple-trees stood in blossom, and the syringas scented the air and hung their long green branches down into the winding canal. Oh, it was so beautiful there, in the freshness of spring! And from the thicket came three beautiful white swans. They rustled their feathers, and swam lightly on the water. The duckling recognized the majestic birds, and was seized with a strange melancholy. 'I will fly to them, those royal birds, and they will kill me, because I, who am so ugly, dare to approach them. But it does not matter; better to be killed by them than to be bitten by the ducks, pecked by the chickens, kicked by the girl who feeds the poultry, and to have so much to suffer in winter!' So he flew into the water, and swam towards the beautiful swans. They saw him, and shot forward to meet him with ruffled feathers. 'Kill me!' said the poor bird, and bowed his head low, expecting death. But what did he see in the water? He saw his own image, and lo! it was no longer a clumsy, dark-grey bird, ugly and hateful to look at, but a graceful and beautiful swan! It does not matter that one has been born in a duck-yard, if one has only lain in a swan's egg. He felt quite glad that he had endured so much trouble and misfortune, for now he had a fuller understanding of his own happiness, and the large swans swam round him, and stroked him with their beaks. Some little children came into the garden with bread and corn, which they threw into the water; and the smallest cried out: 'There is a new one!' And the other children shouted with joy: 'Yes, a new one has come!' And they clapped their hands and danced about, and ran to their father and mother; and bread and cake were thrown into the water; and they all said: 'The new one is the most beautiful of all! So young and handsome!' And the old swans bowed their heads before him. Then he felt quite ashamed, and hid his head under his wing, for he did not know what to do. He was too happy, but not at all proud, for a good heart never becomes proud. He thought of how he had been persecuted and despised, and now he heard them all say that he was the most beautiful of all beautiful birds. And the syringas bent their branches down into the water before him, and the sun shone warm and mild. Then his wings rustled, his slender neck was raised, and from his heart he cried rejoicingly: 'I never dreamed of so much happiness when I was the ugly duckling!'

And the other children shouted with joy: 'Yes, a new one has come!' And they clapped their hands and danced about, and ran to their father and mother; and bread and cake were thrown into the water; and they all said: 'The new one is the most beautiful of all! So young and handsome!' And the old swans bowed their heads before him. Then he felt quite ashamed, and hid his head under his wing, for he did not know what to do. He was too happy, but not at all proud, for a good heart never becomes proud. He thought of how he had been persecuted and despised, and now he heard them all say that he was the most beautiful of all beautiful birds. And the syringas bent their branches down into the water before him, and the sun shone warm and mild. Then his wings rustled, his slender neck was raised, and from his heart he cried rejoicingly: 'I never dreamed of so much happiness when I was the ugly duckling!'

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
description: Two swindlers sell the Emperor invisible clothes; a child speaks the truth.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Many years ago there was an Emperor so exceedingly fond of new clothes that he spent all his money on being well dressed. He cared nothing about reviewing his soldiers, going to the theatre, or going for a ride in his carriage, except to show off his new clothes. He had a coat for every hour of the day, and instead of saying, as one might, about any other ruler, 'The King's in council,' here they always said, 'The Emperor's in his dressing room.' In the great city where he lived, life was always gay. Every day many strangers came to town, and among them one day came two swindlers. They let it be known they were weavers, and they said they could weave the most magnificent fabrics imaginable. Not only were their colors and patterns uncommonly fine, but clothes made of this cloth had a wonderful way of becoming invisible to anyone who was unfit for his office, or who was unusually stupid. 'Those would be just the clothes for me,' thought the Emperor. 'If I wore them I would be able to discover which men in my empire are unfit for their posts. And I could tell the wise men from the fools. Yes, I certainly must get some of the stuff woven for me right away.' He paid the two swindlers a large sum of money to start work at once. They set up two looms and pretended to weave, though there was nothing on the looms. All the finest silk and the purest old thread which they demanded went into their traveling bags, while they worked the empty looms far into the night. 'I'd like to know how those weavers are getting on with the cloth,' the Emperor thought, but he felt slightly uncomfortable when he remembered that those who were unfit for their position would not be able to see the fabric. It couldn't have been that he doubted himself, yet he thought he'd rather send someone else to see how things were going. The whole town knew about the cloth's peculiar power, and all were impatient to find out how stupid their neighbors were. 'I'll send my honest old minister to the weavers,' the Emperor decided. 'He'll be the best one to tell me how the material looks, for he's a sensible man and no one does his duty better.' So the honest old minister went to the room where the two swindlers sat working at their empty looms. 'Heaven help me,' he thought as his eyes flew wide open, 'I can't see anything at all!' But he did not say so. Both the swindlers begged him to be so kind as to come near to approve the excellent pattern, the beautiful colors. They pointed to the empty looms, and the poor old minister stared as hard as he dared. He couldn't see anything, because there was nothing to see. 'Heaven have mercy,' he thought. 'Can it be that I'm a fool? I'd have never guessed it, and not a soul must know. Am I unfit to be the minister? It would never do to let on that I can't see the cloth.' 'Well, sir, you don't say anything about the cloth,' said one of the weavers. 'Oh, it's beautiful! It's enchanting!' said the old minister, peering through his spectacles. 'Such a pattern, what colors!' I'll be sure to tell the Emperor how delighted I am with it.' 'We're pleased to hear that,' said the swindlers. They proceeded to name all the colors and to explain the intricate pattern. The old minister paid the closest attention, so that he could tell it all to the Emperor. And so he did. The swindlers at once asked for more money, more silk and gold thread, to get on with the weaving. But it all went into their pockets. Not a thread went into the looms, though they worked at their weaving as hard as ever. The Emperor presently sent another trustworthy official to see how the work progressed and how soon it would be ready. The same thing happened to him that had happened to the minister: he looked and he looked, but as there was nothing to see in the looms he couldn't see anything. 'Isn't it a beautiful piece of goods?' said the two swindlers, showing and explaining the beautiful pattern and colors which were not there. 'I know I'm not stupid,' the man thought, 'so it must be that I'm unworthy of my good office! That's strange. I mustn't let anyone find it out, though.' So he praised the material he did not see. He declared he was delighted with the beautiful colors and the exquisite pattern. To the Emperor he said, 'It held me completely enchanted.' All the town was talking of this splendid cloth, and the Emperor wanted to see it for himself while it was still in the looms. Attended by a band of chosen men, among whom were his two old trusted officials — the ones who had been to the weavers — he set out to see the two swindlers. He found them weaving with might and main, but without a thread in their looms. 'Magnificent!' said the two officials already duped. 'Just look, Your Majesty, what colors! What a design!' They pointed to the empty looms, each supposing that the others could see the stuff. 'What's this?' thought the Emperor. 'I can't see anything. This is terrible! Am I a fool? Am I unfit to be the Emperor? What a thing to happen to me of all people!' 'Oh! It's very pretty,' he said. 'It has my highest approval.' And he nodded approbation, and gazed on the empty looms. Nothing could make him say that he couldn't see anything. His whole retinue stared and stared. One saw no more than another, but they all joined the Emperor in exclaiming, 'Oh! It's beautiful!' They advised him to wear clothes made of this wonderful cloth at the great procession which was soon to take place. 'Magnificent! Excellent! Unsurpassed!' were bandied from mouth to mouth, and everyone did his best to seem well pleased. The Emperor gave each of the swindlers a cross to wear in his buttonhole, and the title of 'Sir Weaver.' The swindlers stayed up all night before the day of the procession, burning sixteen candles, so that everyone could see how anxious they were to finish the Emperor's new suit. They pretended to take the cloth off the loom. They made cuts in the air with huge scissors. And at last they said, 'Now the Emperor's new clothes are ready for him!' Then the Emperor himself came with his noblest courtiers, and the swindlers each raised an arm as if they were holding something. They said, 'These are the trousers, here's the coat, and this is the mantle,' naming each garment. 'All of them are as light as a spider web. One would almost think he had nothing on, but that's what makes them so fine.' 'Exactly,' all the courtiers agreed, though they could see nothing, for there was nothing to see. 'If Your Imperial Majesty will condescend to take your clothes off,' said the swindlers, 'we will help you on with your new ones here in front of the great mirror.' The Emperor undressed, and the swindlers pretended to put his new clothes on him, one garment after another. They took him around the waist and seemed to be fastening something — that was his train — and the Emperor turned round and round before the looking glass. 'How well Your Majesty's new clothes look. Aren't they becoming!' he heard on all sides. 'That pattern, so perfect! Those colors, so suitable! It is a magnificent outfit.' Then the minister of public processions announced: 'Your Majesty's canopy is waiting outside.' 'Well, I'm supposed to be ready,' the Emperor said, and turned again for one last look in the mirror. 'It is a remarkable fit, isn't it?' He seemed to regard his costume with the greatest interest. The noblemen who were to carry his train stooped low and reached for the floor as if they were picking up his mantle. Then they pretended to lift and hold it high. They didn't dare admit they had nothing to hold. So off went the Emperor in procession under his splendid canopy. Everyone in the streets and the windows said, 'Oh, how fine are the Emperor's new clothes! Don't they fit him to perfection? And see his long train!' Nobody would confess that he couldn't see anything, for that would prove him either unfit for his position, or a fool. No costume the Emperor had worn before was ever such a complete success. 'But he hasn't got anything on,' a little child said. 'Did you ever hear such innocent prattle?' said its father. And one person whispered to another what the child had said, 'He hasn't anything on. A child says he hasn't anything on.' 'But he hasn't got anything on!' the whole town cried out at last. The Emperor shivered, for he suspected they were right. But he thought, 'This procession has got to go on.' So he walked more proudly than ever, as his noblemen held high the train that wasn't there at all.

title: The Little Match Girl
description: A freezing match-seller's visions carry her to her grandmother on New Year's Eve.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: It was dreadfully cold; it was snowing fast, and was almost dark, as evening came on — the last evening of the year. In this cold and darkness there went along the street a poor little girl, bareheaded, and with naked feet. When she left home she had slippers on, it is true; but what was the good of that? They were very large slippers, which her mother had hitherto worn; and they dropped off her feet as she hurried across the street, when two carriages rattled by terribly fast. One slipper was nowhere to be found; the other had been laid hold of by an urchin, and off he ran with it; he thought it would do capitally for a cradle when he some day had children of his own. So the little maiden walked on with her tiny naked feet, that were quite red and blue from cold. She carried a quantity of matches in an old apron, and she held a bundle of them in her hand. Nobody had bought anything of her the whole livelong day; no one had given her a single farthing. She crept along trembling with cold and hunger — a very picture of sorrow, the poor little thing! The flakes of snow covered her long fair hair, which fell in pretty curls around her neck; but of that, of course, she never thought. The lights were shining from every window, and there was a savory smell of roast goose, for it was New-year's eve — yes, she remembered that. In a corner, between two houses, one of which projected beyond the other, she sank down and huddled herself together. She had drawn her little feet under her, but she could not keep off the cold; and she dared not go home, for she had sold no matches, and could not bring home even a penny of money. Her father would certainly beat her; besides, it was almost as cold at home as here, for they had only the roof to cover them, through which the wind howled, although the largest holes had been stopped up with straw and rags. Her little hands were almost frozen with the cold. Ah! perhaps a burning match might be some good, if she could draw it from the bundle and strike it against the wall, just to warm her fingers. She drew one out — 'scratch!' how it sputtered as it burnt! It gave a warm, bright light, like a little candle, as she held her hand over it. It was really a wonderful light. It seemed to the little girl that she was sitting by a large iron stove, with polished brass feet and a brass ornament. How the fire burned! and seemed so beautifully warm that the child stretched out her feet as if to warm them, when, lo! the flame of the match went out, the stove vanished, and she had only the remains of the half-burnt match in her hand. She rubbed another match on the wall. It burst into a flame, and where its light fell upon the wall it became as transparent as a veil, and she could see into the room. The table was covered with a snowy white table-cloth, on which stood a splendid dinner service, and a steaming roast goose, stuffed with apples and dried plums. And what was still more wonderful, the goose jumped down from the dish and waddled across the floor, with a knife and fork in its breast, to the little girl. Then the match went out, and there remained nothing but the thick, damp, cold wall before her. She lighted another match, and then she found herself sitting under a beautiful Christmas-tree. It was larger and more beautifully decorated than the one which she had seen through the glass door at the rich merchant's. Thousands of tapers were burning upon the green branches, and colored pictures, like those she had seen in the show-windows, looked down upon it all. The little one stretched out her hand towards them, and the match went out. The Christmas lights rose higher and higher, till they looked to her like the stars in the sky. Then she saw a star fall, leaving behind it a bright streak of fire. 'Someone is dying,' thought the little girl, for her old grandmother, the only one who had ever loved her, and who was now dead, had told her that when a star falls, a soul was going up to God. She again rubbed a match on the wall, and the light shone round her; in the brightness stood her old grandmother, clear and shining, yet mild and loving in her appearance. 'Grandmother,' cried the little one, 'O take me with you; I know you will go away when the match burns out; you will vanish like the warm stove, the roast goose, and the large, glorious Christmas-tree.' And she made haste to light the whole bundle of matches, for she wished to keep her grandmother there. And the matches glowed with a light that was brighter than the noon-day, and her grandmother had never appeared so large or so beautiful. She took the little girl in her arms, and they both flew upwards in brightness and joy far above the earth, where there was neither cold nor hunger nor pain, for they were with God. In the dawn of morning there lay the poor little one, with pale cheeks and smiling mouth, leaning against the wall; she had been frozen to death on the last evening of the year; and the New-year's sun rose and shone upon a little corpse! The child still sat, in the stiffness of death, holding the matches in her hand, one bundle of which was burnt. 'She tried to warm herself,' said some. No one imagined what beautiful things she had seen, nor into what glory she had entered with her grandmother, on New-year's day.

title: The Tinderbox
description: A soldier's magic tinderbox summons three mighty dogs and wins him a princess.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.text: A soldier came marching along the high road: 'Left, right — left, right.' He had his knapsack on his back, and a sword at his side; he had been to the wars, and was now returning home. As he walked on, he met a very frightful-looking old witch in the road. Her under-lip hung quite down on her breast, and she stopped and said: 'Good evening, soldier; you have a very fine sword, and a large knapsack, and you are a real soldier, so you shall have as much money as you like.' 'Thank you, old witch,' said the soldier. 'Do you see that large tree?' said the witch, pointing to a tree beside them. 'Well, it is quite hollow inside, and you must climb to the top, when you will see a hole, through which you can let yourself down into the tree to a great depth. I will tie a rope round your body, so that I can pull you up again when you call out to me.' 'But what am I to do, down in the tree?' asked the soldier. 'Get money,' she said; 'for you must know that when you get to the ground under the tree, you will find yourself in a large hall, lighted up by three hundred lamps; you will then see three doors, which can be opened easily, for the keys are in all the locks. On going into the first of the chambers, to which these doors lead, you will see a large chest, standing in the middle of the floor, and upon it a dog seated, with a pair of eyes as large as teacups. But you need not be afraid of him; I will give you my blue checked apron, and you must spread it out upon the floor, and then boldly seize hold of the dog, and place him upon it. You can then open the chest, and take from it as many pence as you please, they are only copper pence; but if you would rather have silver money, you must go into the second chamber. Here you will find another dog, with eyes as big as mill-wheels; but do not let that trouble you. Place him upon my apron, and then take what money you please. If, however, you like gold better, go into the third chamber, where you will find another chest full of it. The dog that sits on this money chest is very dreadful; his eyes are as big as a tower, but do not mind him. If he also is placed upon my apron, he cannot hurt you, and you may take from the chest what gold you will.' 'This is not a bad story,' said the soldier; 'but what am I to give you, old witch? for, of course, you do not mean to tell me all this for nothing.' 'No,' said the witch; 'but I do not ask for a single penny. Only promise to bring me an old tinderbox, which my grandmother left behind the last time she went down there.' 'Very well; I promise. Only tie the rope round my body,' said the soldier. 'Take my blue checked apron,' said the witch. So the soldier climbed the tree, and let himself down through the hole till he came to the ground. And there he found, as the witch had told him, the large hall, in which many hundred lamps were burning. Then he opened the first door. 'Ah!' there sat the dog, with the eyes as large as teacups, staring at him. 'You are a pretty fellow,' said the soldier, seizing him, and placing him on the witch's apron, while he filled his pockets from the chest with as many copper coins as they would hold. Then he closed the lid, seated the dog upon it again, and walked into another chamber, And, sure enough, there sat the dog with eyes as big as mill-wheels. 'You had better not look at me in that way,' said the soldier; 'you will make your eyes water;' and then he seated him also upon the apron, and opened the chest. But when he saw what a quantity of silver money it contained, he very quickly threw away all the coppers he had taken, and filled his pockets and his knapsack with nothing but silver. Then he went into the third chamber, and there he was obliged to hold his breath with amazement. The dog in this chamber had eyes indeed as large as towers, and they turned round and round in his head like wheels. 'Good morning to you,' said the soldier, touching his cap, for he had never seen such a dog in his life. But after looking at him more closely, he thought he had been civil enough, so he placed him on the floor, and opened the chest. Good gracious! what a quantity of gold there was! enough to buy all the sugar-sticks of the sweet-stuff women; all the tin soldiers, whips, and rocking-horses in the world, or even the whole town itself. There was, indeed, an immense quantity. So the soldier threw away all the silver money he had taken, and filled his pockets and his knapsack with gold instead; and not only his pockets and his knapsack, but even his cap and boots, so that he could scarcely walk. He was now really rich. Then he seated the dog upon the chest again, closed the door, and called up through the tree: 'Now pull me up, old witch.' 'Have you got the tinderbox?' asked the witch. 'No, I declare! I quite forgot it.' So he went back and fetched the tinderbox, and then the witch drew him up out of the tree, and he stood again in the high road, with his pockets, his knapsack, his cap, and boots full of gold. 'What are you going to do with the tinderbox?' asked the soldier. 'That is nothing to you,' replied the witch; 'you have the money, now give me the tinderbox.' 'I tell you what,' said the soldier, 'if you don't tell me what you are going to do with it, I will draw my sword and cut off your head.' 'No!' said the witch. The soldier immediately cut off her head, and there she lay. Then he tied all his money in her apron, and slung it on his back like a bundle, and put the tinderbox in his pocket, and walked off to the town. It was a very nice town; and he put up at the very best inn, and ordered a dinner of all his favorite dishes, for now he was rich and had plenty of money. The servant, who cleaned his boots, thought they certainly were a funny pair to belong to such a rich gentleman, for he had not yet bought any new ones. The next day he purchased some good clothes and proper boots, so that our soldier soon became a fine gentleman; and the people told him of all the splendors of the town, and about the King, and what a pretty princess his daughter was. 'How can I get to see her?' asked the soldier. 'She is not to be seen at all,' they said; 'she lives in a large copper castle, surrounded by walls and towers. No one but the King may go in or out, for there has been a prophecy that she will marry a common soldier, and the King cannot bear to think of such a marriage.' 'I should like very much to see her,' thought the soldier; but he could not get permission. However, after a while he spent all his money; and had not a shilling left, and could no longer stay at the inn. So he was obliged to move into a little garret under the roof, and clean his own boots, and even mend them with a large needle. None of his friends came to see him, there were too many stairs to mount. One dark evening, he had not even a penny to buy a candle; then all at once he remembered that there was a piece of candle stuck in the tinderbox, which he had brought from the old tree. He found the box with the candle in it; but no sooner had he struck a few sparks from the flint and steel, than the door flew open, and the dog with eyes as large as teacups, whom he had seen under the tree, stood before him, and said: 'What does my lord command?' 'Good heavens!' said the soldier; 'this is a pleasant tinderbox, if I can get all I want like this.' He asked the dog to bring him some money, and the dog was gone in a flash, and returned with a large bag of coppers. The soldier now knew the value of the tinderbox; if he struck it once, the dog that sat on the chest of copper money made his appearance; if twice, the dog that watched over the silver money came; and if three times, the dog that guarded the gold. The soldier had now plenty of money; he returned to his elegant rooms, and reappeared in his fine clothes, so that his friends knew him again, and made as much of him as before. After a while he began to think it was very strange that no one could get a look at the princess. 'Everyone says she is very beautiful,' thought he to himself; 'but what is the use of that if she is to be shut up in a copper castle surrounded by so many walls and towers. Can I by any means get to see her? Stop! where is my tinderbox?' Then he struck a light, and, presto! there came the dog with eyes as large as teacups. 'It is midnight,' said the soldier, 'yet I should very much like to see the princess, if only for a moment.' The dog was gone in an instant, and before the soldier could wink, he returned with the princess. She was lying on the dog's back asleep, and looked so beautiful, that every one who saw her would know she was a real princess. The soldier could not help kissing her, for he was a true soldier. Then the dog ran back with the princess; but in the morning, when the King and Queen were drinking tea, the princess said, that she had had such a strange dream in the night about a dog and a soldier: that she had ridden on the dog's back, and been kissed by the soldier. 'That is a very pretty story, indeed,' said the Queen. So the next night one of the ladies-in-waiting was to watch by the princess's bed, to discover whether it was really a dream, or what else it might be. The soldier had a great longing to see the princess again; so he sent for the dog in the night to fetch her, and to run with her as fast as he could. But the lady-in-waiting slipped on india-rubber shoes, and followed them as quickly, and saw them disappear into a large house. She thought to herself, 'Now I know where it is,' and made a large cross on the door with a piece of chalk. Then she went home to bed, and the dog presently came back with the princess. But when he saw that a cross had been burned on the door of the house where the soldier lived, he took another piece of chalk and made crosses on all the doors in the town, so that the lady-in-waiting might not be able to find out the right door. Early the next morning the King and Queen, the lady-in-waiting, and all the officers went out to see where the princess had been. 'Here it is,' said the King, when they came to the first door with a cross on it. 'No, it is here,' said the Queen, when she saw the second door also had a cross. 'And here is one, and there is another!' they all exclaimed; for there were crosses on all the doors in every direction. So they felt it would be useless to search further. But the Queen was a very clever woman; she could do a great deal more than merely ride in a carriage. She took her large golden scissors, cut a piece of silk into a neat little bag, and filled it with buckwheat flour. She tied it round the princess's neck, and when she went to bed, she cut a little hole in the bag, so that the flour would be scattered on the ground all the way as the princess went to the soldier's house. In the night, the dog came again and carried the princess on his back to the soldier, who loved her very much, and wished that he had been a prince, so that he might have her for his wife. The dog did not observe how the flour ran out of the bag all the way from the castle wall to the soldier's house, and even up to the window, where he had climbed with the princess. Therefore in the morning the King and Queen found out where their daughter had been, and the soldier was taken up and put in prison. Oh, how dark and disagreeable it was there! And they said to him: 'To-morrow you are to be hanged.' This was not very pleasant news, and he had left his tinderbox at the inn. In the morning he could see through the iron grating of the little window how the people were hurrying out of the town to see him hanged; he heard the drums beating, and saw the soldiers marching. Every one was running out to look at them, and a shoemaker's boy, with leather apron and slippers, was running so fast, that one of his slippers flew off and struck against the wall where the soldier sat looking through the iron grating. 'Hallo, you shoemaker's boy, you need not be in such a hurry,' cried the soldier to him. 'There will be nothing to see till I come; but if you will run to where I have been living, and fetch me my tinderbox, you shall have four shillings, but you must put your best foot foremost.' The shoemaker's boy liked the idea of getting the four shillings, and ran very fast and fetched the tinderbox, and gave it to the soldier. And now we shall see what happened. Outside the town a large gallows had been erected, round which stood the soldiers and many thousands of people. The King and the Queen sat on splendid thrones opposite the judges and the whole council. The soldier already stood on the ladder; but as they were about to put the rope round his neck, he said that an innocent request was often granted to a poor criminal before he suffered death. He wished very much to smoke a pipe, as it would be the last pipe he should ever smoke in the world. The King could not refuse this request, so the soldier took his tinderbox, and struck fire, once, twice, thrice, — and there suddenly stood all three dogs; — the one with eyes as big as teacups, the one with eyes as large as mill-wheels, and the third, whose eyes were as large as towers. 'Help me now, that I may not be hanged,' cried the soldier. And the dogs fell upon the judges and all the council, seized one by the legs, and another by the nose, and tossed them many feet high in the air, so that they fell down and were dashed to pieces. 'I will not be touched,' said the King. But the largest dog seized him, as well as the Queen, and threw them up, following the others. Then the soldiers were afraid, and the people cried out: 'Good soldier, you shall be our king, and you shall marry the beautiful princess.' So they placed the soldier in the King's carriage, and the three dogs danced in front and cried 'hurrah!' and the little boys whistled through their fingers, and the soldiers presented arms. The princess came out of the copper castle, and became queen, which was very pleasing to her. The wedding took place a week afterwards, and the three dogs sat at the table, and stared with their great eyes.

title: Thumbelina
description: A thumb-sized girl escapes toads, beetles and a mole to marry a flower prince.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a woman who wished for a very little child, but she did not know where she could get one. So she went to an old witch, and said to her: 'I should so much like to have a little child; can you tell me where I can get one?' 'Oh, that can easily be managed,' said the witch. 'Here is a barleycorn; it is not of the kind which grows in the farmer's field, or which the chickens get to eat. Put it in a flower-pot, and you shall see what will happen.' 'Thank you,' said the woman, and gave the witch twelve shillings, for that was the price. Then she went home and planted the barleycorn, and immediately there grew up a large and beautiful flower, which looked like a tulip; but its leaves were tightly closed, as if it were still a bud. 'What a beautiful flower!' said the woman, and she kissed the pretty red and yellow leaves; but just as she kissed it, the flower gave a loud crack, and opened. It was a real tulip, as one could see; but in the middle of the flower there sat a tiny little girl, sweet and pretty, and she was not larger than a thumb; so she was called Thumbelina. She got an elegant polished walnut-shell for her cradle, blue violet-leaves for her mattress, and a rose-leaf for her coverlet. There she slept at night, but in the day-time she played on the table, where the woman had put a plate with a wreath of flowers round it, the stems of which stood in water; on it floated a large tulip-leaf, and on this Thumbelina sat, and sailed from one side of the plate to the other, rowing herself with two white horsehairs for oars. It was a charming sight. She could sing too, and in so soft and sweet a voice as had never been heard before. One night, when she was lying in her pretty bed, a large, ugly, wet toad came hopping in at the window, in which there was a broken pane. 'Ugh!' said the toad, 'what a pretty little wife this would make for my son.' So she seized the walnut-shell, in which Thumbelina was asleep, and hopped away with it through the window into the garden. There flowed a broad stream; but the bank was marshy and muddy, and here the toad lived with her son. Ugh! how ugly he was too, just like his mother. 'Koax, koax, brekekekex,' was all he could say when he saw the pretty little girl in the shell. 'Don't talk so loud, or she will wake,' said the old toad; 'she might run away from us, for she is as light as a bit of swan's-down. We will put her on one of the broad water-lily leaves out in the stream; it will be just like an island to her, she is so small and light; then she cannot get away, and we can prepare the state-room under the marsh, where you are to live with your wife.' Out in the stream there were a great many water-lilies, with broad green leaves, which looked as if they were floating on the water. The leaf farthest away was the largest, and the old toad swam out to it, and put the walnut-shell, with Thumbelina in it, upon it. The poor little thing woke up very early in the morning, and when she saw where she was, she began to cry bitterly, for there was water on every side of the large green leaf, and she could not get to land. The old toad was down in the marsh, decking out her room with rushes and yellow marigold leaves, to make it smart for the new daughter-in-law; and then she swam out with her ugly son to the leaf on which Thumbelina was. She wanted to fetch the pretty cradle, that she might put it in the bridal room before going to Thumbelina herself. def word_count():
    return sum(len(c["text"].split()) for c in BOOK["chapters"])

def print_book(ch=None):
    print("=" * 64)
    print(BOOK["title"].upper(), "\nby", BOOK["author"], "-", BOOK["genre"])
    print("=" * 64)
    for c in BOOK["chapters"]:
        if ch and c["n"] != ch:
            continue
        print("\n\nCHAPTER %d: %s\n%s" % (c["n"], c["title"], "-" * 40))
        print(c["text"])
    print("\n[%d words, %d chapters — complete]" % (word_count(), len(BOOK["chapters"])))

def search(word):
    w = word.lower()
    for c in BOOK["chapters"]:
        for i, para in enumerate(c["text"].split("\n\n")):
            if w in para.lower():
                print("[ch %d, para %d] %s..." % (c["n"], i + 1, para[:160].replace("\n", " ")))

def write_html(path="book.html"):
    parts = ["<html><head><meta charset='utf-8'><title>%s</title></head><body>" % _h.escape(BOOK["title"])]
    parts.append("<h1>%s</h1><p><i>by %s — %s</i></p>" % (_h.escape(BOOK["title"]), _h.escape(BOOK["author"]), _h.escape(BOOK["genre"])))
    for c in BOOK["chapters"]:
        parts.append("<h2>Chapter %d: %s</h2>" % (c["n"], _h.escape(c["title"])))
        for para in c["text"].split("\n\n"):
            parts.append("<p>%s</p>" % _h.escape(para))
    parts.append("</body></html>")
    open(path, "w").write("\n".join(parts))
    print("wrote", path)

author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.text: In China, as you know, the Emperor is Chinese, and all the people round him are Chinese too. It is many years ago since the story I am going to tell you happened, but that is all the more reason for telling it, lest it should be forgotten. The Emperor's palace was the most splendid in the whole world; it was made entirely of the finest porcelain, very costly, but so brittle and delicate that you had to take great care how you touched it. In the garden there were the most beautiful flowers, and on the most splendid of them were tied little silver bells, which rang, so that no one should pass by without noticing them. Yes, everything in the Emperor's garden was very fine, and it extended so far that even the gardener did not know the end of it. If you went on, you came to a splendid forest with tall trees and deep lakes. The wood extended right down to the sea, which was deep and blue; large ships could sail under the branches of the trees, and in the branches lived a Nightingale, which sang so deliciously that even the poor fisherman, who had so much else to do, lay still to listen to it when he went out at night to cast his nets. 'How beautiful that is!' said he, but he was obliged to attend to his work, and forgot it. But when in the night he heard it again, he said: 'How beautiful that is!' From all the countries of the world travelers came to the Emperor's town, and admired it, and the palace, and the garden; but when they heard the Nightingale, they said: 'That is the best of all!' And the travelers told about it when they went home, and learned men wrote many books about the town, the palace, and the garden; and they did not forget the Nightingale, which was praised most highly; and the poets wrote the most beautiful verses about the Nightingale in the wood by the sea. These books were circulated through the world, and some of them at last reached the Emperor. He sat in his golden chair, and read and read; every moment he nodded his head, for it pleased him to read the splendid descriptions of the town, the palace, and the garden. 'But the Nightingale is the best of all!' it said. 'What is that?' exclaimed the Emperor. 'The Nightingale! I don't know it at all! Is there such a bird in my empire, and even in my garden? I have never heard of it. I must learn about such things from books!' Then he called his gentleman-in-waiting, who was so grand that if any one of lower rank than his dared to speak to him or ask him a question, he only said 'P!' and that means nothing. 'They say there is a very wonderful bird called a Nightingale here,' said the Emperor. 'They say it is the best thing in all my great empire. Why have I never been told anything about it?' 'I have never heard it mentioned,' said the gentleman-in-waiting. 'I will seek it out, and find it.' 'But where is the Nightingale to be found?' asked the gentleman-in-waiting, and ran up and down all the staircases in the palace, through halls and corridors, but no one he met had ever heard of the Nightingale. Then the gentleman-in-waiting ran back to the Emperor, and said that it must be a fable invented by the writers of the books. 'Your Imperial Majesty must not believe all that is written; books are often mere inventions, even if they are not what we call black art.' 'But the book in which I read it,' said the Emperor, 'was sent to me by the great and mighty Emperor of Japan, so it cannot be untrue. I will hear the Nightingale! It must be here this very evening! I extend to it my most gracious favor! And if it does not come, the whole court shall be trampled upon after supper!' 'Tsing-pe!' said the gentleman-in-waiting, and ran up and down all the staircases again, through all the halls and corridors, and half the court ran with him, for they did not want to be trampled upon. There was much questioning about the wonderful Nightingale, which all the world knew except those at court. At last they found a poor little kitchen-maid in the kitchen. She said: 'Oh heavens, the Nightingale! I know it well; yes, how it can sing! Every evening I am allowed to carry the broken victuals to my poor sick mother, who lives down by the sea. On my way back, when I am tired, I rest a little in the wood, and then I hear the Nightingale sing. The tears come into my eyes, and it is just as if my mother kissed me.' 'Little kitchen-maid,' said the gentleman-in-waiting, 'I will procure you a high position in the kitchen, and you shall have permission to see the Emperor at dinner, if you will lead us to the Nightingale, for it is announced for this evening.' So they all went out to the wood where the Nightingale was wont to sing; half the court went. When they were well on the way, a cow began to low. 'Oh!' said the court pages, 'now we have it! That is certainly a wonderful power in so small an animal! I have certainly heard it before.' 'No, that is a cow lowing,' said the little kitchen-maid. 'We are still far from the place.' Then the frogs began to croak in the marsh. 'Splendid!' said the Chinese court chaplain; 'it sounds just like little church bells.' 'No, those are frogs,' said the little kitchen-maid. 'But I think we shall soon hear it now.' Then the Nightingale began to sing. 'That is it!' said the little kitchen-maid. 'Listen, listen! There it sits!' And she pointed to a little grey bird up in the branches. 'Is it possible?' said the gentleman-in-waiting. 'I should never have thought it was like that. How common it looks! Seeing so many grand people must surely have frightened away its colors.' 'Little Nightingale!' called out the little kitchen-maid quite loud, 'our gracious Emperor wishes you to sing before him.' 'With the greatest pleasure,' said the Nightingale, and sang so deliciously that it was a pleasure to listen. 'It sounds just like glass bells,' said the gentleman-in-waiting. 'And look at its little throat, how it moves! It is wonderful that we have never heard it before. I am sure it will be a great success at court.' 'Shall I sing again before the Emperor?' asked the Nightingale, who thought the Emperor was there. 'My precious little Nightingale,' said the gentleman-in-waiting, 'I have the great pleasure to invite you to a court festival this evening, where his Gracious Imperial Majesty desires to be charmed with your delightful singing.' 'It sounds best among the trees,' said the Nightingale; but it came willingly when it heard the Emperor wished it. There was great decorating at the palace. The walls and the floors, which were of porcelain, shone in the light of many thousand golden lamps. The most beautiful flowers, which could ring, were placed in the corridors. There was hurrying and running, and the great bell rang, so that one could not hear one's own voice for it. In the middle of the great hall, where the Emperor sat, a golden perch had been placed, on which the Nightingale was to sit. The whole court was there, and the little kitchen-maid had got permission to stand behind the door, for she had now the title of cook. Everyone was in full dress, and everyone looked at the little grey bird, to whom the Emperor nodded. And the Nightingale sang so deliciously that the tears came into the Emperor's eyes, and the tears ran down his cheeks; and then the Nightingale sang still more beautifully, till its song touched all hearts. And the Emperor was so delighted that he said the Nightingale should have his golden slipper to wear round its neck. But the Nightingale declined with thanks; it had already received a sufficient reward. 'I have seen tears in the Emperor's eyes,' it said; 'that is the greatest reward to me. An emperor's tears have wonderful power. I am rewarded enough.' And then it sang again with its sweet, glorious voice. 'That is the most charming coquetry I have ever seen,' said the ladies, and they took water in their mouths to gurgle when any one spoke to them, thinking they could imitate the Nightingale. Even the lackeys and the chambermaids said they were satisfied, which is saying a great deal, for they are the hardest to please. In short, the Nightingale was a great success. It was now to remain at court, to have its own cage, with liberty to go out twice a day and once at night. It was given twelve servants, who all held a silken string fastened round its leg, and held it tight when it went out. There was not much pleasure in an outing of that kind. The whole town was talking about the wonderful bird, and when two people met, one said to the other: 'Nightin,' and the other said 'gale,' and then they sighed, without understanding each other. And eleven cheesemongers' children were named after it, but not one of them could sing a note. One day the Emperor received a large parcel, on which was written 'The Nightingale.' 'Here is another new book about our celebrated bird,' said the Emperor. But it was not a book; it was a work of art in a box — an artificial nightingale, which was to sing like the real one. It was covered all over with diamonds, rubies, and sapphires; and as soon as it was wound up, it could sing one of the pieces the real Nightingale sang; and it wagged its tail, which glittered with silver and gold. Round its neck hung a little ribbon, on which was written: 'The Emperor of China's Nightingale is poor compared with the Emperor of Japan's.' 'That is splendid!' they all said, and the bringer of the artificial bird immediately received the title of 'Imperial Nightingale-Bringer-in-Chief.' 'Now they must sing together; what a duet that will be!' So they had to sing together, but they did not get on very well, for the real Nightingale sang in its own way, and the artificial bird could only sing waltzes. 'It is not its fault,' said the music-master; 'it keeps very good time, and that is just as it should be.' Then the artificial bird had to sing alone. It was just as successful as the real one, and besides, it was much prettier to look at; it glittered like bracelets and breast-pins. Three-and-thirty times it sang the same piece without being tired. The people would gladly have heard it again, but the Emperor said the real Nightingale should now sing a little. But where was it? No one had noticed that it had flown out of the open window, away to its green woods. 'What is this?' said the Emperor. And all the courtiers scolded, and said the Nightingale was a very ungrateful bird. 'But we have the best bird,' said they, and the artificial bird had to sing again, and that was the thirty-fourth time they heard the same piece. But they did not know it quite by heart, for it was very difficult. And the music-master praised the bird tremendously, and said it was better than the real one, not only in its plumage and the many beautiful diamonds, but in its singing too. 'For you see, ladies and gentlemen, with the real Nightingale you never know what will come, but with the artificial bird everything is settled. It will be so, and so it is! You can account for it, you can take it to pieces, and show the human ingenuity in its construction, how the wheels go, how they turn, and so on.' 'Those are just my thoughts,' they all said, and the music-master got permission to show the bird to the people on the next Sunday. They were to hear it sing too, said the Emperor. And they heard it, and were as delighted as if they had drunk themselves merry with tea, for that is quite Chinese. And they all said 'Oh!' and held up their forefingers and nodded. But the poor fishermen, who had heard the real Nightingale, said: 'It sounds pretty, and it is very like the real one, but there is something wanting, I don't know what.' The real Nightingale was banished from the empire. The artificial bird had its place on a silken cushion close to the Emperor's bed. All the presents it had received, gold and precious stones, lay round it, and it had risen to the title of 'High Imperial Singer of the Table,' and to the rank of Number One on the left; for the Emperor considered that the left side, on which the heart is, was the most distinguished, and the heart of an emperor is on the left, as with other people. And the music-master wrote five-and-twenty volumes about the artificial bird; the work was very learned and long, full of the hardest Chinese words, and every one said he had read and understood it, for otherwise they would have been stupid, and would have been trampled upon. So things went on for a whole year. The Emperor, the court, and all the other Chinese knew every little twitter in the artificial bird's song by heart. But just for that reason it pleased them best; they could sing with it themselves, and they did so. The street boys sang 'Tra-la-la-la-la,' and the Emperor sang it too. Oh, it was delightful! But one evening, when the artificial bird was singing its best, and the Emperor lay in bed listening to it, something snapped inside the bird: 'Whirr!' Something sprang, and the wheels ran round, and then the music stopped. The Emperor jumped out of bed, and had his own physician sent for; but what could he do? Then the clockmaker was sent for, and after a great deal of talk and examination, he got the bird into something like order; but he said it must be very sparingly used, for the pegs were worn, and it would be impossible to put in new ones in such a way as to make it play as before. There was great mourning, for the artificial bird could now only be played once a year, and even that was a strain upon it. But the music-master made a little speech full of hard words, and said it was just as good as before, and so it was just as good as before. Now five years had passed, and a great sorrow came upon the land. The Chinese really loved their Emperor, and he now lay so ill that it was said he could not live. Already a new emperor had been chosen, and the people stood in the street and asked the gentleman-in-waiting how the old Emperor was. 'P!' said he, and shook his head. The Emperor lay pale and cold in his great splendid bed. The whole court thought he was dead, and every one ran to pay homage to the new Emperor. The chamberlains ran out to talk about it, and the ladies'-maids had company to coffee. Cloth had been laid down in all the halls and passages, so that no footstep should be heard, and therefore it was quite, quite still. But the Emperor was not dead yet; he lay stiff and pale on the gorgeous bed with the long velvet curtains and the heavy gold tassels. High above him a window had been left open, and the moon shone in upon the Emperor and the artificial bird. The poor Emperor could hardly breathe; it was as if something were sitting on his chest. He opened his eyes, and then he saw that it was Death who sat on his chest, and who had put on his golden crown, and held in one hand the Emperor's sword, and in the other his splendid banner. And all around, from among the folds of the velvet curtains, strange heads peered forth; some very ugly, some very mild and pleasant. They were all the Emperor's bad and good deeds, which stood now and looked at him, while Death sat on his heart. 'Do you remember this?' whispered one after another. 'Do you remember that?' and they told him so much that the sweat ran from his forehead. 'I never knew that!' said the Emperor. 'Music! music!' he cried. 'The large Chinese drum, that I may not hear what they say!' But they went on, and Death nodded like a Chinaman to all they said. 'Music! music!' cried the Emperor. 'You precious little golden bird, sing, I pray you! I have given you gold and precious stones; I have hung my golden slipper round your neck; sing, I pray you, sing!' But the bird stood silent; there was no one to wind it up, and without that it could not sing. And Death continued to stare at the Emperor with his great hollow eyes, and all was silent, terribly silent. Suddenly, close to the window, the most lovely song was heard — the real, living Nightingale, sitting on a branch outside. It had heard of the Emperor's illness, and had come to sing to him of comfort and hope. And as it sang, the phantoms grew paler and paler; the blood coursed with fresh vigor through the Emperor's weak limbs, and even Death listened and said: 'Go on, little Nightingale, go on!' 'Will you give me the splendid golden sword? Will you give me the rich banner? Will you give me the Emperor's crown?' said Death. And Death gave up each of them for a song. And the Nightingale went on singing; it sang of the quiet churchyard, where the white roses grow, where the elder-blossom smells sweet, and the fresh grass is wet with the tears of the living. Then Death felt a longing to see his garden, and floated out of the window in the form of a cold, white mist. 'Thanks, thanks, you heavenly little bird!' said the Emperor. 'I know you! I banished you from my empire, and yet you have sung the evil faces away from my bed, and driven Death from my heart. How can I reward you?' 'You have rewarded me already,' said the Nightingale. 'I brought tears to your eyes the first time I sang to you; I shall never forget that. Those are the jewels that rejoice a singer's heart. But sleep now, and wake fresh and strong! I will sing to you.' And it sang, and the Emperor fell into a sweet sleep. Oh, how mild and refreshing that sleep was! The sun shone in at his window in the morning, when he awoke strong and well. None of his servants had come back yet, for they thought he was dead; but the Nightingale was still singing. 'You must always stay with me,' said the Emperor. 'You shall sing when you like, and I will break the artificial bird into a thousand pieces.' 'Do not do that,' said the Nightingale. 'It did its best as long as it could. Keep it as before. I cannot live in the palace and build my nest; but let me come when I like. Then I will sit in the evening on the branch by the window, and sing to you, so that you may be glad and thoughtful too. I will sing of the happy and of those who suffer; I will sing of good and of evil, which are hidden from you. The little singing bird flies far around, to the poor fisherman, to the peasant's roof, to all who are far from you and your court. I love your heart better than your crown, and yet the crown has a scent of something holy about it. I will come and sing to you. But you must promise me one thing.' 'Everything!' said the Emperor, who now stood in his imperial robes, which he had put on himself, and held his heavy golden sword against his heart. 'One thing I beg of you: do not tell any one that you have a little bird who tells you everything. Then things will go all the better.' And the Nightingale flew away. The servants came in to look at their dead Emperor — and, lo! there he stood, and said: 'Good morning!'
