title: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
description: A one-legged tin soldier loves a paper dancer through fire and water.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There were once five-and-twenty tin soldiers, who were all brothers, for they had been made out of the same old tin spoon. They shouldered arms and looked straight before them. Their uniform was red and blue and very splendid. The first thing in the world they ever heard was the word 'Tin soldiers!' uttered by a little boy, who clapped his hands with delight when the lid of the box, in which they lay, was taken off. They were given him for a birthday present, and he stood at the table to set them up. The soldiers were all exactly alike, except one, who had only one leg; he had been left to the last, and then there had not been enough melted tin to finish him, so they made him to stand firmly on one leg, and this caused him to be very remarkable. The table on which the tin soldiers stood, bore many other playthings, but the most attractive to the eye was a pretty little paper castle. Through the small windows the rooms could be seen. In front of the castle a little mirror was lying, which was intended to represent a lake, and swans made of wax swam on it and were mirrored in it. All this was very pretty, but the prettiest of all was a tiny little lady, who stood at the open door of the castle; she, also, was made of paper, and she wore a dress of clear muslin, with a narrow blue ribbon over her shoulders just like a scarf. In front of these was fixed a glittering tinsel rose, as large as her whole face. The little lady was a dancer, and she stretched out both her arms, and raised one of her legs so high, that the tin soldier could not see it at all, and he thought that she, like himself, had only one leg. 'That is the wife for me,' he thought; 'but she is too grand, and lives in a castle, while I have only a box to live in, and there are five-and-twenty of us in that. It is no place for her. Still I must try and make her acquaintance.' Then he laid himself at full length on the table behind a snuff-box that stood upon it, so that he could peep at the little delicate lady, who continued to stand on one leg without losing her balance. When evening came, the other tin soldiers were all placed in the box, and the people of the house went to bed. Then the playthings began to have their own games together, to pay visits, to have sham fights, and to give balls. The tin soldiers rattled in their box; they wanted to get out and join the amusements, but they could not open the lid. The nut-crackers played at leap-frog, and the pencil jumped about the table. There was such a noise that the canary woke up and began to talk, and in verse too. Only the tin soldier and the dancer remained in their places. She stood on tiptoe, with her legs stretched out, as firmly as he did on his one leg. He never took his eyes from her for a moment. The clock struck twelve, and, with a bounce, up sprang the lid of the snuff-box; but, instead of snuff, there jumped up a little black goblin; for the snuff-box was a toy puzzle. 'Tin soldier,' said the goblin, 'don't stare at things that don't concern you.' But the tin soldier pretended not to hear. 'Just you wait till to-morrow!' said the goblin. When the children came in the next morning, they placed the tin soldier in the window. Now, whether it was the goblin or the draught, all at once the window flew open, and the tin soldier fell headlong from the third story into the street beneath. It was a terrible fall; he came to stand on his head, his bayonet stuck in between the flagstones, and his one leg in the air. The servant maid and the little boy went down stairs directly to look for him; but he was nowhere to be seen, although once they nearly trod upon him. If he had called out, 'Here I am!' it would have been all right, but he was too proud to cry out for help while he wore a uniform. Presently it began to rain, and the drops fell faster and faster, till there was a heavy shower. When it was over, two boys happened to pass by, and one of them said, 'Look, there is a tin soldier. He ought to have a boat to sail in.' So they made a newspaper into a boat, and set the tin soldier in the middle of it, and the two boys ran along by the side of it, and clapped their hands. 'Good heavens! what waves there are, and what a current!' said they; but the paper boat rocked up and down, and turned round and round so fast that the tin soldier trembled; still he remained firm; his countenance did not change; he looked straight before him, and shouldered his musket. Suddenly the boat shot under a bridge which formed a part of a drain, and then it was as dark as the tin soldier's box. 'Where am I going now?' thought he. 'This is the black goblin's fault, I am sure. Ah, well, if the little lady were only here with me in the boat, I would not care if it were twice as dark.' Suddenly there appeared a great water-rat, who lived in the drain. 'Have you a passport?' asked the rat, 'give it to me at once.' But the tin soldier remained silent and held his musket tighter than ever. The boat sailed on and the rat followed it. 'How he gnashes his teeth! How he calls out to the floating sticks and straws: 'Stop him, stop him! he has not paid toll! He has not shown his pass!'' But the stream rushed on stronger and stronger. The tin soldier could already see daylight shining where the arch ended. Then he heard a roaring sound quite terrible enough to frighten the bravest man. At the end of the tunnel the drain fell into a large canal, and that would have been as dangerous a thing for him as for us to be carried down a great waterfall. He was too close to it to stop, so the boat rushed on, and the poor tin soldier held himself as stiffly as he could, without moving an eyelid. The boat whirled round three or four times, and was filled with water to the brim; nothing could save it from sinking. He now stood up to his neck in water, while deeper and deeper sank the boat, and the paper became soft and loose with the wet, till at last the water closed over the soldier's head. He thought of the elegant little dancer whom he should never see again, and the words of the song sounded in his ears: 'Farewell, warrior! ever brave, drifting onward to thy grave.' Then the paper boat fell to pieces, and the tin soldier sank through the water and was swallowed by a great fish. Oh, how dark it was inside the fish! It was darker even than the tunnel, and very narrow too. But the tin soldier bore it, and lay at full length shouldering his musket. The fish danced about and made the most extraordinary movements. At last it became quite still. After a while, a flash of lightning seemed to pass through it, and then the daylight shone in, and a voice said: 'The tin soldier!' The fish had been caught, taken to the market and sold to the cook, who had taken it into the kitchen and cut it open with a large knife. She picked up the soldier between two fingers, and carried him into the room, where all were anxious to see the remarkable man who had traveled about in the stomach of a fish. But the tin soldier was not at all proud. They placed him on the table, and — how many curious things may happen in the world! — the tin soldier was in the very same room as before; he saw the same children, and the same toys stood on the table, and there was the pretty castle with the elegant little dancer at the door. She was still standing on one leg, and held the other in the air. She, also, was steadfast. The tin soldier was so touched to see her that he almost wept tin tears, but he kept them back. He only looked at her, and they both remained silent. Presently one of the little boys took up the tin soldier, and threw him into the stove. He gave no reason for this strange conduct. It must have been the fault of the goblin in the snuff-box. The flames lighted up the tin soldier most fearfully, and he felt a terrible heat; but whether the heat was the result of the real fire, or of the love he felt, he did not know. He had lost his splendid colors; it might have been from his perilous voyage, or it might have been from grief; no one could tell. He looked at the little lady, and she looked at him; and he felt himself melting away, but he still remained firm, with his musket on his shoulder. Suddenly the door of the room flew open, and the draught of air caught up the little dancer, and she fluttered like a sylph right into the stove, to the tin soldier, and was instantly seized by the flames and was gone. Then the tin soldier melted down into a lump, and the next morning, when the maid servant took the ashes out of the stove, she found him in the shape of a little tin heart. But of the little dancer nothing remained but the tinsel rose, which was burnt as black as a cinder.

title: The Red Shoes
description: Vain Karen cannot stop dancing in her cursed red shoes.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a little girl who was very pretty and delicate, but in summer she was forced to go barefoot, she was so poor, and in winter she wore very large wooden shoes, which made her little insteps quite red, and that looked so dangerous. In the middle of the village lived an old shoemaker's wife; she sat and sewed together, as well as she could, a little pair of shoes out of old red strips of cloth. They were very clumsy, but it was a kind intention, and the little girl was to have them. The little girl was called Karen. On the very day that her mother was buried, she received the red shoes, and wore them for the first time. They were certainly not suitable for mourning, but she had no others, and so she walked in them with bare legs behind the poor coffin. Just then a large old carriage came by, and in it sat a large old lady; she looked at the little girl, and felt compassion for her, and then she said to the clergyman: 'Give me the little girl, and I will take care of her.' And Karen believed that all this happened on account of the red shoes; but the old lady thought they were horrible, and they were burnt. But Karen herself was dressed very neatly and cleanly; she was taught to read and to sew, and people said she was a pretty little thing. But the mirror said: 'You are more than pretty — you are beautiful!' One day the Queen was traveling through the country, and she had her little daughter with her, who was a princess. The people flocked towards the castle, and Karen was there too; and the little princess stood in her fine white dress in a window, and let herself be stared at; she had neither a train nor a golden crown, but she wore splendid red morocco shoes; they were certainly far handsomer than those the shoemaker's wife had made for little Karen. Nothing in the world can be compared with red shoes! Karen was now old enough to be confirmed; she had new clothes, and was to have new shoes. The rich shoemaker in the town took the measure of her little foot in his own room, in which there stood great glass cases full of pretty shoes and shining boots. It was a charming sight, but the old lady could not see well, and so had no pleasure in it. Among the shoes stood a pair of red ones, just like those the princess had worn. How beautiful they were! The shoemaker said also that they had been made for a count's daughter, but that they had not fitted her. 'That must be patent leather,' said the old lady; 'they shine so.' 'Yes, they shine so,' said Karen, and they fitted her, and were bought. But the old lady did not know that they were red, for she would never have allowed Karen to be confirmed in red shoes, as she was now to be. Everybody looked at her feet; and when she stepped through the chancel door on the church pavement, it seemed to her as if the old figures on the tombs, those portraits of old preachers and their wives, with stiff ruffs, and long black dresses, fixed their eyes on her red shoes, and she thought only of them as the clergyman laid his hand upon her head, and spoke of the holy baptism, of the covenant with God, and how she should now be a grown-up Christian. And the organ pealed so solemnly, and the sweet children's voices sang, and the old music-director sang, but Karen thought only of her red shoes. In the afternoon the old lady was told by everybody that the shoes were red, and she said that it was very wrong of Karen, that it was not at all becoming, and that in future Karen should only go to church in black shoes, even if they were old. The next Sunday there was the sacrament, and Karen looked at the black shoes, and she looked at the red ones — and then she looked at the red ones again, and put the red ones on. It was beautiful sunny weather; Karen and the old lady went through the cornfields; it was rather dusty there. At the church-door stood an old soldier with a crutch, and with a wonderfully long beard; it was more red than white, and he bowed to the ground, and asked the old lady whether he might dust her shoes. And Karen stretched out her little foot too. 'See, what beautiful dancing shoes!' said the soldier; 'sit fast, when you dance,' said he, addressing the shoes, and slapping the soles with his hand. And the old lady gave the soldier alms, and went into the church with Karen. And all the people in the church looked at Karen's red shoes, and all the pictures looked at them; and as Karen knelt before the altar, and put the cup to her mouth, she thought only of the red shoes, and they seemed to swim in it; and she forgot to sing the psalm, and she forgot to say 'Our Father.' Now all the people went out of church, and the old lady got into her carriage. Karen raised her foot to get in after her, when the old soldier said: 'Look, what beautiful dancing shoes!' and Karen could not help it, she was obliged to dance a few steps; and when she had once begun, her legs continued to dance; the shoes would not stop; she danced round the church corner, she could not leave off; the coachman had to run and catch hold of her, and he lifted her into the carriage, but her feet continued to dance, so that she trod on the old lady dreadfully. At length she took the shoes off, and then her legs left off dancing. At home the shoes were put into the cupboard, but Karen could not help looking at them. Now the old lady was sick, and it was said she could not recover. Karen had to nurse and wait upon her, but there was to be a great ball in the town, and Karen was invited. She looked at the old lady, who could not recover; she looked at the red shoes, and she thought there could be no sin in it; she put the red shoes on; that might be allowed too. But then she went to the ball, and began to dance. When she wanted to dance to the right, the shoes danced to the left, and when she wanted to dance up the room, the shoes danced down the room, down the stairs, through the street, and out through the town-gate. She danced, and was forced to dance, far out into the dark wood. Something glimmered up among the trees, and she thought it was the moon, for it was a face. It was the old soldier with the red beard; he sat there, nodded his head, and said: 'Look, what beautiful dancing shoes!' She was frightened, and wanted to throw the red shoes away; but they clung fast; and she tore off her stockings, but the shoes had grown fast to her feet. And she danced, and was forced to dance, over fields and meadows, in rain and sunshine, by night and day; but by night it was the most fearful. She danced over the churchyard, but the dead there did not dance; they had something better to do than that. She would have liked to sit down on the poor man's grave, where the bitter tansy grew; but for her there was neither rest nor repose. And when she danced towards the open church-door, she saw an angel standing there. He wore long, white garments; he had wings which reached from his shoulders to the earth; his countenance was severe and grave; and in his hand he held a broad shining sword. 'Thou shalt dance!' said he, 'dance in thy red shoes till thou art pale and cold, till thy skin shrivels up and thou art a skeleton! Thou shalt dance from door to door, and wherever proud, vain children live thou shalt knock, so that they may hear thee and fear thee! Thou shalt dance —' 'Mercy!' cried Karen. But she did not hear what the angel answered, for the shoes carried her through the gate into the fields, along highways and byways, and she was forced to dance continually. One morning she danced past a door she knew well, and heard a psalm sung within; then a coffin was carried out, strewn with flowers, and she knew that the old lady was dead, and felt that she was now forsaken by every one, and cursed by the angel of God. She danced, and was forced to dance, through the dark night. The shoes carried her over thorns and stumps, and she was torn till she bled. She danced over the heath till she came to a little house; she knew that the executioner lived here, and she tapped with her finger on the panes, and said: 'Come out! come out! I cannot come in, for I am forced to dance.' And the executioner put his head out of the window, and said: 'Don't you know who I am? I strike off the heads of wicked people, and I feel that my axe is tingling to do so.' 'Don't cut my head off,' said Karen, 'for then I could not repent of my sin. But cut off my feet with the red shoes.' And then she confessed all her sin, and the executioner cut off her feet with the red shoes; but the shoes danced away with the little feet across the field into the deep forest. And he carved her a pair of wooden feet, and crutches, and taught her a psalm, which the criminals always sing; and she kissed the hand which had wielded the axe, and went over the heath. 'Now I have suffered enough for the red shoes,' said she; 'now I will go to church, that they may see me.' And she went as fast as she could to the church-door; but when she came there, the red shoes danced before her, and she was frightened, and turned back. The whole week she was sad, and wept many bitter tears; but when Sunday came, she said: 'Now I have suffered and struggled enough. I believe I am just as good as many of those who sit in church and hold their heads so high.' And then she went boldly on; but she had not got farther than the churchyard gate before she saw the red shoes dancing before her, and she was frightened, and turned back, and repented of her sin from her heart. And she went to the parsonage, and begged that she might be taken into service there. She would be industrious, she said, and would do everything that she could; she did not care about the wages, only she wanted a roof over her, and to be with good people. And the clergyman's wife had pity on her, and took her into service. And she was industrious and thoughtful. She sat still and listened when the clergyman read the Bible in the evening. All the children loved her very much, but when they spoke of dress, and splendor, and beauty, she shook her head. The next Sunday they all went to church, and they asked her if she would go with them; but she looked sadly, with tears in her eyes, at her crutches. They were certainly not suitable for mourning, but she had no others, and so she walked in them with bare legs behind the poor coffin. Just then a large old carriage came by, and in it sat a large old lady; she looked at the little girl, and felt compassion for her, and then she said to the clergyman: 'Give me the little girl, and I will take care of her.' And Karen believed that all this happened on account of the red shoes; but the old lady thought they were horrible, and they were burnt. But Karen herself was dressed very neatly and cleanly; she was taught to read and to sew, and people said she was a pretty little thing. But the mirror said: 'You are more than pretty — you are beautiful!' One day the Queen was traveling through the country, and she had her little daughter with her, who was a princess. The people flocked towards the castle, and Karen was there too; and the little princess stood in her fine white dress in a window, and let herself be stared at; she had neither a train nor a golden crown, but she wore splendid red morocco shoes; they were certainly far handsomer than those the shoemaker's wife had made for little Karen. It was a charming sight, but the old lady could not see well, and so had no pleasure in it. Among the shoes stood a pair of red ones, just like those the princess had worn. How beautiful they were! At the church-door stood an old soldier with a crutch, and with a wonderfully long beard; it was more red than white, and he bowed to the ground, and asked the old lady whether he might dust her shoes. And Karen stretched out her little foot too. 'See, what beautiful dancing shoes!' said the soldier; 'sit fast, when you dance,' said he, addressing the shoes, and slapping the soles with his hand. title: The Princess and the Pea
description: A true Princess feels three peas through twenty mattresses.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a Prince who wished to marry a Princess; but she must be a real Princess. He travelled all over the world in hopes of finding such a lady; but there was always something wrong. Princesses he found in plenty; but whether they were real Princesses it was impossible for him to decide, for now one thing, now another, seemed to him not quite right about the ladies. At last he returned to his palace quite cast down, because he wished so much to have a real Princess for his wife. One evening a fearful tempest arose, it thundered and lightened, and the rain poured down from the sky in torrents: besides, it was as dark as pitch. All at once there was heard a violent knocking at the door, and the old King, the Prince's father, went out himself to open it. It was a Princess who was standing outside the door. What with the rain and the wind, she was in a sad condition; the water trickled down from her hair, and her clothes clung to her body. She said she was a real Princess. 'Ah! we shall soon see that!' thought the old Queen-mother; however, she said not a word of what she was going to do; but went quietly into the bedroom, took all the bed-clothes off the bed, and put three little peas on the bedstead. She then laid twenty mattresses one upon another over the three peas, and put twenty feather beds over the mattresses. Upon this the Princess was to pass the night. The next morning she was asked how she had slept. 'Oh, very badly indeed!' she replied. 'I have scarcely closed my eyes the whole night through. I do not know what was in my bed, but I had something hard under me, and am all over black and blue. It has hurt me so much!' Now it was plain that the lady must be a real Princess, since she had been able to feel the three little peas through the twenty mattresses and twenty feather beds. None but a real Princess could have such a delicate sense of feeling. The Prince accordingly made her his wife; being now convinced that he had found a real Princess. The three peas were however put into the cabinet of curiosities, where they are still to be seen, provided they are not lost. Wasn't this a story with a meaning?

title: The Swineherd
description: A proud princess trades kisses for trinkets and loses a prince.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a poor Prince; he had a kingdom, but it was a very small one. Still it was large enough to marry upon, and he wished to marry. It was certainly rather bold of him to say to the Emperor's daughter: 'Will you marry me?' But he did venture to say so, for his name was famous far and wide; and there were a hundred princesses who would have answered 'Yes,' and thanked him, too. But the Emperor's daughter, we shall see what she said. Now let us listen. On the grave of the Prince's father there grew a rose-tree — a most beautiful rose-tree. It bloomed only once in five years, and then it bore but a single rose, but, oh, such a rose! Its perfume was so sweet that whoever smelt it forgot all his cares and sorrows. And the Prince had also a nightingale, which could sing as if all the sweet melodies in the world were in its little throat. This rose and this nightingale the Princess was to have; and therefore they were both put into silver cases, and sent to her. The Emperor had them carried before him into the great hall, where the Princess was playing at 'visiting' with her ladies-in-waiting; and when she saw the cases with the presents, she clapped her hands for joy. 'Ah, if it were but a little pussy-cat!' said she. But the rose-tree with its beautiful rose came to view. 'Oh, how prettily it is made!' said all the court ladies. 'It is more than pretty,' said the Emperor, 'it is charming!' But the Princess touched it, and was almost ready to cry. 'Fie, papa!' said she. 'It is not made at all, it is natural!' 'Let us see what is in the other case, before we get into a bad humor,' said the Emperor. So the nightingale came forth and sang so delightfully that at first no one could say anything ill-humored of it. 'Superbe! Charmant!' exclaimed the ladies; for they all used to chatter French, each one worse than the other. 'How much the bird reminds me of the musical box of the late lamented Empress,' said an old courtier. 'Oh! the very same tone, the same execution.' 'Yes! yes!' said the Emperor, and he wept like a child at the remembrance. 'I will hope that it is not a real bird,' said the Princess. 'Yes, it is a real bird,' said those who had brought it. 'Well, then, let the bird fly,' said the Princess; and she positively refused to see the Prince. But he was not to be discouraged; he smeared his face over with black and brown, pulled his cap over his ears, and knocked at the door. 'Good day to the Emperor,' said he. 'Can I have employment here in the palace?' 'Why, there are so many applicants for places,' said the Emperor, 'but let me see — I want some one to look after the pigs, for we have a great many of them.' So the Prince was appointed 'Imperial Swineherd.' He had a dirty little room to live in close by the pigsty; and there he sat the whole day and worked. By the evening he had made a pretty little saucepan. All round it were little bells, and when the pot was boiling, they tinkled in the most charming way, and played the old melody: 'Ach! du lieber Augustin, Alles ist weg, weg, weg!' But what was still more curious, whoever held his finger in the steam of this saucepan, immediately smelt all the dishes that were cooking on every hearth in the city — this, you see, was something quite different from a real rose. Now the Princess happened to walk that way; and when she heard the tune, she stood quite still, and seemed pleased; for she could play 'Lieber Augustin'; it was the only one she knew; and she played it with one finger. 'Why, there is my piece,' said she. 'This swineherd must certainly have been well educated! Go in and ask him the price of the instrument.' So one of the ladies-in-waiting had to go in; however, she drew on wooden slippers first. 'What will you take for the saucepan?' said the lady. 'I will have ten kisses from the Princess,' said the swineherd. 'Heaven forbid!' said the lady. 'I will have ten kisses from the Princess,' said the swineherd. 'Well, you may tell him that,' said the Princess. 'But you must stand before me so that no one can see it.' So the ladies stood in front of her, and spread out their dresses, and the swineherd got ten kisses, and the Princess — the saucepan. Then the Princess was delighted! She danced round and round, and all the evening she did nothing but hold the saucepan; for in it, you know, were all the dishes cooking in the town. The ladies danced about and clapped their hands. 'We know who is going to eat sweet soup and pancakes for dinner to-morrow. We know who is going to have hash and sausages; who is going to have such and such things!' 'Yes, but keep my secret, for I am an Emperor's daughter.' The swineherd — that is to say — the Prince, for no one knew that he was other than an ill-favored swineherd, let not a day pass without working at something; and at last he made a rattle, which, when it was swung round, played all the waltzes and jig tunes which have ever been heard since the creation of the world. 'That is superb!' said the Princess, when she passed by. 'I have never heard prettier music. Go in and ask him the price of the instrument.' 'I will have a hundred kisses from the Princess,' said the swineherd. 'He is mad,' said the Princess, and walked on, but she stopped to listen once more. 'I think I shall go in,' she said to her ladies. So one of the ladies had to go in again. 'A hundred kisses from the Princess,' said he. 'I think he is mad,' said the Princess. 'But I shall not tell papa. Go and stand before me, as you did before, so that no one can see.' And the ladies stood round her and spread out their dresses, and the swineherd got the hundred kisses, and the Princess — the rattle. When the Emperor, who was resting, heard the rattle, he came out in his slippers and dressing-gown; but the Princess had slipped off the balcony, and was gone. 'What is that music in the pigsty?' said he. And he went in. 'Why, it is the swineherd!' But he drew back, and put his slippers on, for he had come out in his bare feet. When he got to the pigsty, he quietly put on his spectacles. 'What!' said the ladies, when they saw what was going on; and they were all shocked. 'What!' said the Emperor, when he saw the Princess kissing the swineherd for the rattle. So he boxed the Princess's ears with his slipper, and the swineherd was dismissed, and the Princess too. Then the Prince washed his face, threw off his dirty clothes, and stepped forth in his princely robes; he looked so handsome that the Princess could not help bowing to him. 'I have come to despise thee,' said he. 'Thou wouldst not have an honest prince! Thou couldst not appreciate the rose and the nightingale, but thou couldst kiss the swineherd for the sake of a rattle and a saucepan! Thou art rightly served.' He then went back to his own little kingdom, and shut the door of his palace in her face. Now she might well sing: 'Ach! du lieber Augustin, Alles ist weg, weg, weg!'

title: The Flying Trunk
description: A merchant's son flies in a trunk to woo a Turkish princess with stories.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a merchant who was so rich that he could pave the whole street with gold, and would even then have enough left for a small alley. But he did not do it; he knew how to use his money differently. If he spent a shilling, he got back a crown: such a clever merchant he was — till he died. His son inherited all the money, and he lived merrily; he went every night to the theatre, made paper kites out of bank-notes, and played at ducks and drakes on the sea with gold pieces instead of stones. In this way the money might soon be spent, and so it was. At last he had nothing left but four shillings, and no clothes to wear but a pair of slippers and an old dressing-gown. His friends now did not trouble themselves any more about him, as they could not walk with him in the street; but one of them, who was good-natured, sent him an old trunk, with the message, 'Pack up!' That was all very well, but he had nothing to pack, so he seated himself in the trunk. It was a curious trunk. If the lock was pressed, the trunk could fly. He pressed it, and, whirr! away flew the trunk with him up the chimney, high into the clouds, farther and farther away. The bottom cracked, which was very alarming, for if it had broken in pieces, he would have fallen down in a dreadful manner! But it held, and he arrived in the land of the Turks. title: The Wild Swans
description: A silent sister weaves nettle shirts to free her eleven swan-brothers.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.text: Far away in the land to which the swallows fly when it is winter, dwelt a king who had eleven sons, and one daughter, named Eliza. The eleven brothers were princes, and each went to school with a star on his breast, and a sword by his side. They wrote upon slates of diamond with golden pencils, and learnt their lessons very well. Their sister Eliza sat on a little stool of plate-glass, and had a picture-book which had cost half a kingdom. Oh, these children were very happy; but it was not to remain so always. Their father, who was king of the country, married a very wicked queen, who did not love the poor children at all. They knew this on the very first day after the wedding. In the palace there was a great feast, and the children played at receiving company; but instead of having the cakes and roasted apples which they used to have, the new queen gave them only some sand in a saucer, and told them to pretend it was something good. The week after, she sent the little sister Eliza into the country to a peasant and his wife to be nursed; and not long after she told the king so many untrue things about the eleven princes, that he no longer cared for them. 'Fly out into the world and get your own living,' said the wicked queen. 'Fly like great birds without a voice.' But she could not make it so bad for them as she would have liked, for they were turned into eleven beautiful wild swans. With a strange cry, they flew out of the palace windows, far over the park and the wood. It was early morning when they passed over the peasant's cottage where their sister Eliza lay asleep. They hovered over the roof, turned their long necks, and flapped their wings, but no one heard or saw them. They were obliged to fly on, high up in the clouds, far away into the wide world, till they came to a great dark wood, which stretched to the sea-shore. Poor little Eliza was standing in the peasant's room playing with a green leaf, for she had no other plaything. She pricked a hole in the leaf, and looked through it at the sun, and it seemed to her as if she saw her brothers' clear eyes; and each time the warm sun shone upon her cheeks, she thought of all the kisses they had given her. One day passed just like another. If the wind blew through the great rose-hedge before the house, it would whisper to the roses: 'Who is more beautiful than you?' But the roses would shake their heads and say: 'Eliza is.' And on Sunday, when the peasant's wife sat at the door reading her hymn-book, the wind would turn over the leaves and say to the book: 'Who is more pious and good than you?' 'Eliza is,' said the hymn-book; and the roses and the hymn-book told nothing but the truth. When she was fifteen years old, she returned home. But when the queen saw how beautiful she was, she became angry and envious, and wanted to make her as wicked and ugly as she herself was. First she smeared her with walnut-juice, so that she was quite brown, daubed her face with a nasty ointment, and tangled her beautiful hair. It was impossible to recognize pretty Eliza. When her father saw her, he was much frightened, and said she was not his daughter. No one but the watch-dog and the swallows knew her, and they were only poor animals and could say nothing. Then poor Eliza wept, and thought of her eleven brothers, who were all gone. Sorrowfully she crept out of the palace, and walked the whole day over fields and moors till she came to the great forest. She did not know whither she was going, but she felt so sad for her brothers, who, like herself, had been driven out into the world, that she was determined to seek them. Night came on, and she had quite lost her way. Then she lay down on the soft moss, said her evening prayer, and leaned her head against a stump. All was still and quiet in the wood, the air was so mild, and hundreds of glow-worms shone like green fire among the grass and the moss. When she awoke in the morning, and put aside the branches, she started; for close by she heard the rippling of water. There was a large lake with the most beautiful clear water in it. She bathed her face and hands in it, till she was fair and white again. Then she wandered on in the wood, not knowing whither she went. She saw the wild apples hanging on the trees, and ate of them to satisfy her hunger. Then she asked the reeds and the rushes which way her brothers had gone, but none of them knew. Towards evening she came to a peasant's hut; she peeped in at the window, and saw an old woman within. 'Good evening,' said Eliza to her; but the old woman only nodded, and said nothing. Then Eliza asked her the way to her brothers, but the old woman shook her head. All night Eliza dreamed of her brothers; they were all children again, playing together, writing with their golden pencils on the diamond slates, and looking at the beautiful picture-book which had cost half a kingdom. In her dream they were just as they used to be. When she awoke, the sun was high in the heavens. She could not see the old woman, so she went down to the water and bathed. Suddenly she heard the sound of swans' wings rustling in the air. She started up; the sun was just rising, and close by she saw eleven wild swans, with crowns on their heads, flying towards the land one behind the other, like a long white ribbon. Eliza ran down the slope to the shore, and hid herself behind the bushes. The swans alighted close by her, and flapped their great white wings. As soon as the sun had risen higher in the heavens, the swan's feathers suddenly fell off, and eleven handsome princes, her brothers, stood before her. She uttered a loud cry, for though they were much changed, she knew them, she felt sure they must be her brothers. And she sprang up and threw herself on their necks, and called them each by name. And the princes were delighted when they saw their little sister again, for they knew her, although she had grown tall and beautiful. They laughed and wept, and soon understood how wickedly their stepmother had behaved to them all. 'We brothers,' said the eldest, 'fly about as wild swans as long as the sun is in the heavens; but as soon as it sinks behind the hills, we recover our human shape. Therefore we must always be on the lookout for a safe resting-place for the night, for if we were flying towards the clouds when the sun set, we should fall down into the deep sea. We do not live here, but in a land just as fair, that lies beyond the sea; the way is long, we have to cross the great sea, and there is no island on our way where we could pass the night; we have only a little rock, just large enough for us to rest upon. If the sea is rough, the foam dashes over us; but we thank God even for this rock; we have spent whole nights there, weeping. Our youngest brother, who is still the most tender, cannot fly so far as we can, and therefore we take it in turns to carry him on our backs. But now we cannot stay here longer than to-morrow, for the sea is calm, and we must fly away.' 'Shall we ever be set free?' asked Eliza. 'Yes,' said her brothers, 'but on one condition. You must not speak or laugh for — shall we tell you? — for six years you must be dumb. And in that time you must sew for us eleven shirts of nettles. If a single word passes your lips before the work is finished, we shall die by it. Remember this.' And with these words they flew away. Eliza trembled, and her tears fell upon her hands. 'My dear brothers, I will do everything to set you free,' she whispered. She went into a churchyard, and gathered nettles, and carried them home. With her delicate hands she wove the nettles into flax, and then sewed the eleven shirts. She neither spoke nor laughed. A whole year passed, and she had finished one shirt. Then a king came hunting in the forest. He saw the beautiful dumb girl, and fell in love with her, and took her home to his palace and married her, although his courtiers murmured, and the archbishop himself whispered that she must be a witch. But the king would not listen. Eliza continued her work in secret, even in the palace. The nettles stung her hands till they bled, but she bore it gladly for her brothers' sake. At last the archbishop accused her of witchcraft, and the king, in his grief, consented that she should be burnt. On the morning of her execution, she had finished ten shirts; the eleventh still wanted one sleeve. She was led to the stake, still working, and the crowd mocked her. Then came a rustling of swans' wings; her eleven brothers flew down, and she threw the shirts over them. As the nettle shirts touched them, they became princes again — except the youngest, who had a swan's wing instead of an arm, because one sleeve was unfinished. Then Eliza spoke, and told all, and the king rejoiced, and they lived happily ever after.

If the sea is rough, the foam dashes over us; but we thank God even for this rock; we have spent whole nights there, weeping. Our youngest brother, who is still the most tender, cannot fly so far as we can, and therefore we take it in turns to carry him on our backs. But now we cannot stay here longer than to-morrow, for the sea is calm, and we must fly away.' 'Shall we ever be set free?' asked Eliza. 'Yes,' said her brothers, 'but on one condition. You must not speak or laugh for — shall we tell you? — for six years you must be dumb. And in that time you must sew for us eleven shirts of nettles. If a single word passes your lips before the work is finished, we shall die by it. Remember this.' And with these words they flew away. Eliza trembled, and her tears fell upon her hands. 'My dear brothers, I will do everything to set you free,' she whispered. She went into a churchyard, and gathered nettles, and carried them home. With her delicate hands she wove the nettles into flax, and then sewed the eleven shirts. She neither spoke nor laughed. A whole year passed, and she had finished one shirt. Then Eliza spoke, and told all, and the king rejoiced, and they lived happily ever after.

title: The Shadow
description: A man's detached shadow returns as a rich gentleman and destroys him.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: It is in the hot countries that the sun burns; there the people become quite a mahogany color, and in the very hottest countries they are negroes. But it was only to the hot countries that a learned man from the cold countries had gone; he thought he could wander about there just as he did at home, but he soon found out his mistake. He, and all sensible people, had to stay within doors; the shutters and doors were closed the whole day; it looked as if the whole house were asleep, or there was no one at home. The narrow street with the high houses, in which he lived, was so situated that the sun shone upon it morning and evening with burning heat; it was really unbearable. The learned man from the cold countries — he was a young man, and seemed to be a clever man — sat in a glowing oven; it took effect upon him, he became quite thin, even his shadow shriveled up; the sun took it all away. It did not revive till evening, after the sun had set. It really was a pleasure, as soon as the lights were brought into the room, to see the shadow stretch itself against the wall, for it needed the light to make it strong again. In the evening, when he went out on his balcony, and the stars came forth in the clear, beautiful sky, he felt revived. 'One gets as much amusement as possible in hot countries,' said he, 'but it is a great privation to have no shadow.' And then he felt annoyed that his shadow had shrunk. In the evening, when he went out on the balcony, he stretched himself against the light, for he thought: 'I have no shadow, so I must try to get one.' But it was no use. Then he went into his room, and at last fell asleep. The next morning, when he woke, he went out on the balcony, and there, in the sunshine, lay his shadow — no, it was not his shadow, it was the shadow of the opposite house. Or was it? He looked more closely, and saw that it was his own shadow, which had gone over to the opposite house in the night, and now stood there in the sunshine, as shadows do. 'How strange!' said the learned man. 'My shadow has left me, and gone to live on its own account!' He was very much annoyed, for he knew that a man without a shadow is a very poor creature. In the course of time, however, a new shadow grew out from his feet, for the old one had left a root behind. And the learned man returned to the cold countries, and wrote books about what is true in the world, and what is good and beautiful. Years passed. One evening, as he sat in his room, there was a knock at the door. 'Come in!' said he. And a very thin, tall man walked in — so thin that it was quite painful to look at him. He was dressed in black, and looked like a respectable man. 'Whom have I the honor of speaking to?' asked the learned man. 'I am your old shadow,' said the thin man, 'which you left in the hot countries. I have come to see how you are, and to ask if there is anything I can do for you.' The learned man was very much surprised, but he asked his shadow to sit down. The shadow told him how he had lived in the hot countries, how he had learned everything, and had become a man of the world. He had seen everything, and knew everything. 'But what about your old master?' asked the learned man. 'Oh, he is well,' said the shadow. 'He writes books about the true, the good, and the beautiful. But nobody reads them. I have done better. I have become rich and powerful. I am going to be married to a princess.' The learned man was shocked. 'You cannot marry a princess!' he cried. 'Why not?' said the shadow. 'I am a man like other men. I have a shadow too — a very poor, thin shadow, but still a shadow. And I am rich, and I know the world. The princess will marry me, for she does not know that I was once a shadow.' The learned man tried to reason with his shadow, but it was no use. The shadow had become the master, and the learned man the shadow. In the end, the shadow had the learned man arrested as a madman who claimed to be the master, and the learned man was executed. And the shadow married the princess, and lived in splendor. For in this world, the shadow often becomes more powerful than the man.

title: The Darning Needle
description: A proud darning needle breaks, boasts, and ends in the gutter.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a darning needle who thought herself so fine that she fancied she was an embroidery needle. 'Take care to hold me fast,' she said to the fingers that took her out. 'Don't let me fall; if I fall on the ground, I shall never be found again, I am so fine.' 'It is all right,' said the fingers, and they held her fast. 'See, I am coming with a train,' said the darning needle, as she drew a long thread after her; but there was no knot in the thread. The fingers directed the needle against the cook's slipper, which had burst in the upper leather, and was to be sewn together. 'That is common work,' said the darning needle. 'I shall never get through it. I shall break — I shall break!' And she did break. 'Did I not tell you?' said she. 'I am too fine.' 'Now it is good for nothing,' said the fingers; but they had to hold her fast, nevertheless. The cook dropped some sealing-wax on her, and stuck her in her neckerchief. 'See, now I am a breastpin,' said the darning needle. 'I knew I should come to honor; when one is something, one comes to something.' And she laughed to herself, for one can always see when a darning needle is laughing — she sits so high in her neckerchief, and looks so proud, as if she were in a state coach. 'May I be allowed to ask,' said the pin, who was her neighbor, 'if you are gold?' 'You may,' said the darning needle, 'but you must not speak so loud.' 'I am only common pin,' said the pin, humbly. The darning needle spoke long about her youth, and how fine she had been. Then the cook's slipper broke again, and the darning needle was taken out to sew it. 'This is too common,' said she, and broke again. She was thrown into the gutter. As she lay there, a bottle shard came by, and said: 'You are a fine lady, indeed!' The darning needle, in her pride, fancied she was a breastpin still, and told the shard of her adventures. At last she sank in the mud, and there she lies, still fancying herself fine.

title: The Fir Tree
description: A vain little Fir Tree longs for glory and ends as firewood.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Out in the forest stood a pretty little Fir Tree. It had a good place; the sun shone on it, and the air was fresh around it, but it was not satisfied. 'Oh, how I wish I were as tall as the other trees!' sighed the little Fir. 'Then I would spread my branches far around, and my top would overlook the wide world. The birds would build nests in my branches, and when the wind blew, I would bow gracefully, just like the others.' It took no pleasure in the sunshine, nor in the birds, nor in the red clouds that sailed over it morning and evening. In winter, when the snow lay white around it, a hare would often come hopping over it, and jump right over the little Fir. Oh, that made it so angry! But two winters passed, and when the third came, the little Fir was so tall that the hare had to run round it. 'Oh, to grow, to grow, to get older and taller!' thought the Tree. 'That is the only happiness in the world.' In autumn the woodcutters came and cut down some of the largest trees. The little Fir Tree, which was now quite grown, trembled at the sight, for the splendid large trees fell to the ground with a crash, and their branches were cut off, and they looked so naked and slender. They were put on wagons and drawn by horses out of the forest. 'Where are they going?' asked the little Fir Tree. 'What will become of them?' 'We know! we know!' chirped the sparrows. 'We have looked in at the windows in the town. We know where they go. They are dressed up in the greatest splendor. We have seen them standing in the middle of a warm room, adorned with apples, honey-cakes, toys, and hundreds of candles.' 'And then?' asked the Fir Tree, trembling in all its branches. 'And then what happens?' 'We did not see any more,' said the sparrows. 'But it was splendid!' 'Am I destined for this glorious career?' cried the Fir Tree, rejoicing. 'That is better than crossing the sea! How I long for it! Oh, were it Christmas! Now I am tall and spreading like the others that were carried away last year. Oh, if I were only on the wagon! If I were only in the warm room with all the splendor! And then — yes, then something even better will come, something still grander, or why should they adorn me so? There must be something still grander, still more splendid to come; but what? Oh, I am suffering with longing! I hardly know what is the matter with me!' 'Rejoice in us!' said the air and the sunlight. 'Rejoice in thy fresh youth outdoors!' But the Tree did not rejoice at all; it grew and grew; it was green winter and summer; dark green it was; the people who saw it said: 'That is a handsome tree!' And at Christmas it was cut down before any of the others. The axe cut deep into its marrow, and the Tree fell to the ground with a sigh; it felt a pain, a faintness, and could not think of any happiness, for it was sorry to leave its home, the soil in which it had grown, and it knew that it should never see its dear old companions, the bushes and flowers around it, perhaps not even the birds. The departure was not at all pleasant. The Tree only came to itself when it was unloaded in a courtyard with other trees, and heard a man say: 'This is a splendid one! We want only this.' Then came two servants in handsome livery, and carried the Fir Tree into a large and beautiful room. All around the walls hung pictures, and by the great stove stood large Chinese vases with lions on the covers. There were rocking-chairs, silken sofas, large tables covered with picture-books, and toys worth a hundred times a hundred dollars — at least the children said so. And the Fir Tree was put into a great tub filled with sand; but no one could see that it was a tub, for it was hung round with green cloth, and stood on a large, gayly-colored carpet. Oh, how the Tree trembled! What was to happen now? The servants and the young ladies decked it out. On one branch they hung little nets cut out of colored paper; each net was filled with sweetmeats; golden apples and walnuts hung down as if they grew there; and more than a hundred little candles, red, white, and blue, were fastened to its branches. Dolls that looked exactly like real people — the Tree had never seen such before — fluttered among the leaves, and at the very top was fastened a large gold tinsel star. It was splendid, splendid beyond description. 'This evening,' said they all, 'this evening it will shine!' 'Oh,' thought the Tree, 'that evening will come! Then the candles will be lighted! And what will happen then? Will the trees of the forest come to look at me? Will the sparrows peep in at the windows? Shall I grow fast here, and stand adorned winter and summer?' Of that it knew but little; but it had a great longing, and its bark ached with longing, and that is as bad for a tree as headache is for us. At last the candles were lighted. What splendor! What magnificence! The Tree trembled so in all its branches that one of the candles set fire to a green twig, and it was scorched. 'Heaven help me!' cried the young ladies, and hastily put the fire out. Now the Tree did not dare to tremble at all. Oh, it was terrible! It was so afraid of losing any of its ornaments, and was quite bewildered with all the splendor. And now the folding doors were thrown open, and a crowd of children rushed in as if they would have overturned the Tree. The older people followed more quietly. The little ones stood quite silent, but only for a moment; then they shouted till the room rang; they danced round the Tree, and one present after another was taken from it. 'What are they doing? What will happen now?' thought the Tree. And the candles burned down to the branches, and were put out. Then the children got leave to plunder the Tree. Oh, they rushed upon it so that it cracked in all its joints; if it had not been fastened by its top and by its golden star to the ceiling, it would have fallen down. The children danced about with their pretty toys; no one looked at the Tree, except one old nurse, who came and peeped among the branches, but only to see if a fig or an apple had been forgotten. 'A story! a story!' cried the children, and they drew a little fat man towards the Tree; and he sat down under it, 'for,' said he, 'we are in the greenwood, and the Tree may have the advantage of listening to my story. But I shall only tell one. Will you have the story of Ivedy-Avedy, or of Humpty-Dumpty, who fell downstairs, and yet married the princess and got half a kingdom?' 'Ivedy-Avedy!' cried some, 'Humpty-Dumpty!' cried others, and there was a fine shouting and crying out. But the Fir Tree stood quite silent, and thought: 'Am I to have nothing to do with it? Am I to have no part in it?' For it had been in the evening's amusement, and had done what it could. The man told the story of Humpty-Dumpty, and the Tree stood and listened; the children clapped their hands, and the Tree thought: 'Am I to have nothing to do with it?' At last it was morning. 'Now,' thought the Tree, 'my branches will spread, and I shall be splendid again.' But the servant came and chopped the Tree into small pieces, and threw them on the fire. It burned brightly, and sighed deeply, and each sigh was like a little shot. The children played in the room, and the youngest had a gold star on his breast, which the Tree had worn on its happiest evening. And then the Tree was burned to ashes. And that was the end of the Fir Tree's story.

title: Little Claus and Big Claus
description: Clever Little Claus outwits his brutal namesake with a horse skin and a sack.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: In a village there lived two men who had the same name. They were both called Claus. One of them had four horses, and the other had only one horse; so to distinguish them, people called the owner of the four horses 'Great Claus,' and he who had only one, 'Little Claus.' Now we shall hear what happened to them, for this is a true story. Through the whole week, Little Claus was obliged to plough for Great Claus, and lend him his one horse; and once a week, on a Sunday, Great Claus lent him all his four horses. Then how Little Claus would smack his whip over all five horses, they were as good as five horses to him on that one day. The sun shone brightly, and the church bells were ringing merrily as the people passed by, dressed in their best clothes, with their prayer-books under their arms, to hear the clergyman preach. And they looked at Little Claus ploughing with his five horses, and he was so proud that he smacked his whip, and said, 'Gee-up, my five horses.' 'You must not say that,' said Big Claus; 'for only one of them is yours.' But Little Claus soon forgot what he ought to say, and when any one passed by, he would call out, 'Gee-up, all my horses!' 'Now I tell you not to say that,' said Big Claus; 'for if you say it again, I shall hit your horse on the head, till he is dead; so mind what you say.' 'I will not say it any more,' said Little Claus. But as soon as people came by, nodding to him, and wishing him 'Good day,' he became so proud, and thought how grand it looked to have five horses ploughing in his field, that he smacked his whip, and said, 'Gee-up, all my horses!' 'I'll gee-up your horses for you,' said Big Claus; and seizing a hammer, he struck Little Claus's one horse on the head, and it fell dead instantly. 'Oh, now I have no horse at all,' said Little Claus, weeping. But after a little while he flayed the dead horse, and hung up the skin in the wind to dry. Then he put the dry skin into a bag, and, placing it over his shoulder, went out into the next town to sell the horse's skin. He had a very long way to go, and had to pass through a great dark wood. Presently a storm arose, and he lost his way, and before he discovered the right path, evening came on, and it was too far to go back, and too far to go forward. The storm was so violent that he could scarcely stand. At last he came to a large farmhouse, and knocked at the door, but the farmer's wife said she could not let him in, for her husband was not at home, and she was afraid to admit strangers. Then Little Claus begged to be allowed to lie in the stable; and the woman at last consented. He put his bag under his head in the hay. The stable door was ajar, and through the opening he could see into the room, where a large table was spread with fish, sausages, and wine. The farmer's wife and the sexton were sitting at the table, enjoying themselves. Presently the woman heard her husband coming, and she begged the sexton to hide in a large empty chest, for she was afraid he would be angry if he found him there. The farmer came in, and asked what was for supper. 'Oh, only some bread and cheese,' said the wife. The farmer was angry, and Little Claus in the stable heard everything. Then the farmer's wife knelt down before the oven and took out the roast meats and wine she had hidden, and set them before her husband. Little Claus, seeing the good things, thought of his bag, and pinched the dry horse skin till it squeaked. 'Hush!' said the farmer, 'what is that?' 'It is a wizard in my bag,' said Little Claus. 'He says we need not eat dry bread, for he has conjured the oven full of roast meat and wine.' The farmer opened the oven and found the feast. 'I must buy that wizard,' said he. Little Claus sold the bag with the skin for a bushel of money, and the farmer carried it home. The next day Big Claus killed all his four horses, hoping to sell their skins as well. But when he went to town, the tanners laughed at him, and he had to carry the skins home again. In revenge, he went to Little Claus's house to kill him. Little Claus's old grandmother had just died, and he laid her in his bed, intending to bury her. Big Claus came in the night and struck the 'grandmother' with an axe, thinking it was Little Claus. Horrified at having killed the old woman, Big Claus gave Little Claus a bushel of money to keep quiet. Little Claus put his dead grandmother in a cart and drove to town. At an inn, he made it appear the grandmother was alive, and when the innkeeper's servant spilled hot water on her, Little Claus accused the innkeeper of killing her, and got another bushel of money as compensation. Big Claus, amazed, killed his own grandmother too, hoping for the same, but was beaten and driven out of town. Furious, Big Claus seized Little Claus, put him in a sack, and carried him to the river to drown him. On the way, Big Claus went into a church, leaving the sack by the road. A drover came by with cattle, and Little Claus called out that he was in the sack because he was going to heaven. The drover, wanting to go to heaven, took his place in the sack, and Little Claus drove off with the cattle. Big Claus threw the sack into the river, drowning the drover. When Big Claus returned, he found Little Claus with a herd of cattle. 'Where did you get those?' he asked. 'From the river,' said Little Claus. 'There are plenty of cattle down there.' Greedy Big Claus had himself put in a sack and thrown into the river, and was drowned. And so Little Claus lived happily ever after with his riches.

title: The Girl Who Trod on the Loaf
description: Proud Inger steps on a loaf to save her shoes and sinks to the marsh.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a girl named Inger, who was so proud and haughty that she was ashamed of her poor mother, and would not own her. When she was twelve years old, she went into service with rich people in the country. They dressed her well, and she became prouder than ever. One day her mistress said: 'Inger, you have not been home for a long time; you should go and see your parents. I will give you a large loaf of white bread to take to them; they will be glad to see you.' So Inger put on her best clothes and her new shoes, and started. But the road was muddy, and there were puddles of water. Rather than soil her fine shoes, she threw the loaf into the mud and stepped on it to cross. But the loaf sank with her, deeper and deeper, till she went down into the marsh, to the Marsh Woman, who brews the bog. There she remained, a statue, with the loaf fastened to her feet. The Marsh Woman took her to the devil's grandmother, who keeps the brewery. Inger became a torment to all around her, for her heart had grown as hard as the loaf. She wept no tears, for she could not. Years passed. On earth, her story was told as a warning to proud children. At last, she repented in her heart, and a tear fell. Then she was changed into a little bird, and flew up to the light. She did good, and at last, after long penance, she was forgiven, and flew, a pure soul, to heaven.

title: The Garden of Paradise
description: A prince finds the Garden of Paradise but loses it with a kiss.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a king's son who was very fond of reading, and he had read all the books in his father's library. But he had heard that in the Garden of Paradise the Tree of Knowledge grew, and that whoever ate of its fruit would know everything. So he set out to find the Garden of Paradise. He traveled far, and at last he came to a great forest, where he met an old man who told him the way. After many trials, he reached the Garden, which was guarded by the Fairy of Paradise. She showed him all its wonders: the Tree of Knowledge, the fountain of youth, and all the beautiful flowers. But she warned him: 'You may look at everything, but you must not kiss me, for if you do, the Garden will sink into the earth, and you will never see it again.' The prince promised, but when he saw her beauty, he forgot his promise and kissed her. Then there was a clap of thunder, and the Garden sank. The prince found himself alone in the forest. But he had learned wisdom: that happiness is not in knowing everything, but in doing good. He returned home a wiser man, and ruled his people justly ever after.

title: The Snow Queen
description: Gerda's love melts the ice in Kay's heart and defeats the Snow Queen.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a wicked sprite, the most mischievous of all sprites. One day he made a magic mirror, which had the power of making everything good and beautiful reflected in it shrink to almost nothing, while everything worthless and bad looked larger and uglier. The sprite's scholars ran about with the mirror, and at last they carried it up to heaven to mock the angels. But it fell from their hands and broke into a hundred million pieces, which flew about the world. Some splinters were as large as sand grains, and these flew into people's eyes and hearts, making them see only evil and feel their hearts turn to ice. One such splinter flew into the eye of a little boy named Kay, and another into his heart. Kay lived with his little playmate Gerda, and they loved each other dearly. They had a pretty little garden on the roof, with roses blooming. But after the splinter entered him, Kay became cold and mocking. He mocked Gerda, and mocked the roses. One winter day, Kay went sledging in the square, and tied his little sledge to a large white sledge, which carried him away. It was the Snow Queen's sledge. She wrapped him in her bearskin, kissed him on the forehead — a kiss colder than ice — and the splinter in his heart made him forget Gerda and all his home. She took him to her palace in the far north, where he sat piecing together flat pieces of ice, trying to form the word 'Eternity,' for she had promised him the whole world if he succeeded. When Kay did not come home, Gerda wept, and at last set out to find him. She gave her red shoes to the river, which carried her to an old sorceress's garden, where she was kept for a time among flowers. But the roses reminded her of Kay, and she fled. A crow told her of a princess who had married, thinking the bridegroom might be Kay, but it was not. The prince and princess gave her warm clothes and a golden carriage. Robbers attacked the carriage in the forest, and the robber girl kept Gerda, but at last let her go with her reindeer, Bae. Bae carried her to the far north, to the Finn woman and then the Lapp woman, who told her that Kay was in the Snow Queen's palace, and that the power to free him lay in her loving heart. Gerda reached the palace, and her warm tears melted the splinter in Kay's heart, and her love melted the splinter in his eye. Kay wept, and the splinter washed out. Then they formed the word 'Eternity' with the ice, and the Snow Queen, returning, found her power broken, and let them go. They traveled home, and found that they were grown up, but in their hearts they were still children. And there they sat, on the little stools, in the warm sunshine, among the roses.

title: The Little Mermaid
description: A mermaid trades her voice for legs to love a prince.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower, and as clear as crystal, it is very, very deep. There dwelt the Sea King with his old mother and his six daughters, the sea princesses. The youngest was the most beautiful, with a voice like none other. She loved to hear of the world above, and when she was fifteen, she was allowed to rise to the surface. There she saw a ship, and on it a handsome prince, celebrating his sixteenth birthday. A storm arose, the ship sank, and the little mermaid saved the prince, carrying him to shore. She loved him, but she could not be with him, for she had a fish's tail. So she went to the sea witch, who gave her a draught that would give her legs, but every step would feel as if she trod on sharp knives. Moreover, if the prince married another, she would die and become foam on the sea. The witch cut out her tongue as payment. The little mermaid drank the draught, and woke on the shore with legs, and the prince found her. She stayed with him, dancing though it pained her, but the prince loved another — a princess he thought had saved him. On the wedding morning, her sisters rose from the sea, their hair shorn, and gave her a knife from the witch: if she killed the prince before sunrise, she would live. But she could not. She threw the knife into the sea and cast herself into the waves, becoming foam. But she did not die; she became a daughter of the air, who may win an immortal soul by good deeds.

title: Ole Luk-Oie, the Dream God
description: The Sandman brings a week's worth of dreams to little Hjalmar.
author: Hans Christian Andersen

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There is nobody in the world who knows so many stories as Ole Luk-Oie. He can tell them indeed! In the evening, when the children sit nicely at the table or on their little stools, he comes up the stairs very softly, for he walks in his socks. He opens the doors gently, and, whirr! he squirts sweet milk into their eyes, just a tiny drop, but enough to keep them from opening their eyes. Then he creeps behind them and blows softly on their necks, till their heads begin to nod. Then he has two umbrellas: one with pictures on the inside, which he holds over good children, and then they dream the most beautiful stories all night; and the other, which has no pictures, he holds over naughty children, and they sleep heavily and wake with no dreams. On Monday, he told Hjalmar about the flowers and the garden; on Tuesday, about the pictures on the furniture; on Wednesday, about the little mouse; on Thursday, about the wedding of the dolls; on Friday, about the stars; on Saturday, about his great-grandfather's portrait; and on Sunday — on Sunday he told the most beautiful story of all, about Paradise, and how kind God is. And Hjalmar said: 'I know that story!' And Ole Luk-Oie said: 'Yes, but you have never heard it told properly.' And Hjalmar grew up, and Ole Luk-Oie still visits children every night, with his two umbrellas.
